title: Sean McVay doesn’t want to talk about Rams’ Australia travel plans
summary: Reporter Gary Klein asked Sean McVay about the Los Angeles Rams travel plans for Australia and the head coach wouldn’t answer the question. L.A.‘s head coach is usually very approachable, but in this interaction not so much. McVay just didn’t want to talk about it, so the rumors continue of a quick trip Down Under. […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - JULY 28: Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams speaks with members of the media during training camp at Loyola Marymount University on July 28, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Reporter Gary Klein asked Sean McVay about the Los Angeles Rams travel plans for Australia and the head coach wouldn’t answer the question. L.A.‘s head coach is usually very approachable, but in this interaction not so much. McVay just didn’t want to talk about it, so the rumors continue of a quick trip Down Under. If you’ve followed Klein and McVay, then you’ve seen them have back-and-forth’s like this before, nothing out of the ordinary, but it makes the mind wonder: What are the Rams travel plans for Australia and why the secrecy? McVay is too intentional to not have meaning behind what he does for his football team down to the last detail. He won’t explain the team’s travel plans for Australia, he doesn’t have to and maybe he shouldn’t but in the word of Josh Rosen: Why? Here are today’s top stories about the L.A. Rams. What stands out to you? Sean McVay really doesn’t want to talk about Rams’ Australia plans (ramswire) “ After ESPN reported this week that the Rams will fly into Melbourne only one day before the game, McVay was asked whether the team has finalized its plans for the trip. He declined to answer, and then proceeded to get into a back-and-forth exchange with the reporter about it. Below is the full exchange from Thursday’s press conference. Reporter: “Have you finalized plans for when you guys are going to leave for Australia? How you’re going to handle that trip?” McVay: “Yeah, but I’d rather just keep it in-house.” Reporter: “Why?” McVay: “What’s the reason to talk about it, you know? Honestly, I would respectfully just say we have, but I’d prefer not to talk about it.” Reporter: “Is it a strategic thing?” McVay: “I just don’t want to talk about it. What does it matter?” Reporter: “Well, fans, I think, are curious.” McVay: “We won’t be there long enough for the fans to really have any curiosity about it.” Sean McVay declines to discuss Rams’ plans for Australia travel (nbcsports) “McVay’s comment regarding not being there long enough for the fans to have curiosity seems to confirm that it will indeed be a short trip. Surely, McVay has a reason for not elaborating. Maybe he hasn’t had a chance to fully explain it to the players. Maybe some of them are grumbling about it, and he needs to get them to buy in before he takes it public. Regardless, McVay likely didn’t decide randomly to not address one specific subject. And it’s not as if the Rams will be able to conceal their ultimate itinerary. Everyone will know when they fly to Australia, and everyone will know when they return to L.A.“ Aaron Donald Answers Rams Return Question After Attention-Grabbing Day (heavy.com) The Los Angeles Rams have seen the trend go in their favor regarding Aaron Donald, but the 10-time Pro Bowler has yet to give them a firm answer. There could be a good reason for that. Donald has been away from the game for two years. And while he has remained in shape, getting into peak physical form for the rigors of an NFL season–which the Rams hope ends with a trip to the Super Bowl–is a far different endeavor altogether. Aaron Donald Responds to Question About Rams Return Donald drew attention on Friday, similar to how he did when he was spotted walking off one of the Rams’ practice fields following a workout. This time, Donald was back in LA, but seen working out at UCLA’s facilities. Caught Aaron Donald @ UCLA training today this gives me a feeling he is definitely coming back. My lil nephews asked the question. Let’s go!! @AaronDonald97 #ramshouse #nfl pic.twitter.com/8sD0K4YVln — Poko (@Iampoko_t) August 7, 2026 Moreover, he had on a Rams helmet. There was some debate over whether the footage was recent, though. Some were also unsure if the helmet he had on had white or yellow horns.“ Aaron Donald flew his speed trainer out to LA from Pittsburgh (ramswire) “Donald is going all out to determine whether he wants to play again, pulling out all the stops – from ramping up his training regimen to working out at the Los Angeles Rams’ facility . Sean McVay revealed an interesting tidbit during Thursday’s press conference, telling reporters that Donald flew his usual speed trainer out to Los Angeles from Pittsburgh, which shows how serious he is about this possible return. “He’s got such an intentional routine and rhythm,” McVay said. “He’s had his same speed trainer that he’s worked out with throughout his whole career that he has back at home or back in Pittsburgh that he’s brought out here. He’s taking great care of himself, as we all know. Getting ready to play football and just working out the way that he has, there’s a little bit of a different rhythm and routine. Anything that he does, like I’ve shared with you guys, he’s going to do it with everything that he’s got.” Sean McVay closes out training camp, talks about building depth at each position & looks ahead to the preseason | Inside Rams Camp (therams.com) “Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay joined J.B. Long and D’Marco Farr on this season’s final episode of Inside Rams Camp. The team announced on Friday that it has signed edge rusher Daniel Rickert , bolstering a position that will need some depth during the preseason. Rickert is an undrafted rookie out of the University of Virginia. He played five years at Tennessee Tech before transferring to Virginia in 2025, recording 6.5 sacks and eight tackles for a loss in the 14 games he played for the Cavaliers. After the draft, he received an invite to the Titans’ rookie minicamp but did not sign with the team, leaving him as a free agent.“ LA Rams Roster Moves: • Free Agent Signing DE Daniel Rickert pic.twitter.com/PKNF0aFn13 — Los Angeles Rams (@RamsNFL) August 7, 2026 2026 Rams gameday giveaway and gift with purchase items announced (therams.com) “The MVP returns! title: Raiders training camp: Cousins and Crosby sit out of team sessions
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders had their ninth day at training camp, but it wasn’t without a little drama. The story of the day was that Kirk Cousins and Maxx Crosby were both held out of practice because of their incident on Friday. While they were held out of team sessions such as 11-on-11, both players […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - AUGUST 06: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders practices during the team's training camp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on August 06, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders had their ninth day at training camp, but it wasn’t without a little drama. The story of the day was that Kirk Cousins and Maxx Crosby were both held out of practice because of their incident on Friday. While they were held out of team sessions such as 11-on-11, both players didn’t participate in drills and other parts of practice. The rest day allowed Fernando Mendoza to get first-team reps throughout the morning. Mendoza responded well by having his best day of camp. He was sharp in the red zone period, throwing three touchdowns, with his best throw being to Tre Tucker with great anticipation. The former Heisman Trophy winner ended the day strong during the two-minute drill, completing five passes in a row and helping lead the team to a field goal before time expired. While the trade rumors will fly because of the issues with Crosby and Cousins, it allowed Mendoza to creep up on the starting QB position for Week 1. Mendoza displayed he can work well with the ones and could give Cousins a bigger push for the starting job. Other Camp Notes. -Quay Walker caught my eye today was great against the run but froze in coverage on Bowers’ touchdown -Malik Benson was with the 1’s during the 2-minute drill over Nailor. Nailor had a drop earlier in practice -Mike Washington and Ashton Jeanty are going to be an effective 1-2 punch. Washington showed plenty of explosive runs and is hard to take down at the second level. -Porter looked good in coverage, had a few pass breakups during the day -The offensive line looks improved in the run game, but Malcolm Koonce had a good day against the right tackles. DJ Glaze and Trey Zuhn seem to be in a battle for the spot. -Rogers and JPJ continue to alternate, but Rogers had an injury at the end of practice and didn’t return. -Tonka Hemingway keeps winning day after day; it looks like he is ready to leap. -Stukes was running with 1s and 2s switching with Isaiah Pola-Mao. -Jermod McCoy was with 2s at times and had one of his best days at practice

title: The differences between Raiders kickers Matt Gay and Kansei Matsuzawa
summary: A proven grizzled veteran versus a trailblazing Japanese-born undrafted rookie. That’s the high-level tale of the tape between Matt Gay and Kansei Matsuzawa, the two engaged in a kicker competition for the Las Vegas Raiders this offseason and the fight for place kicker duties and a roster spot is slated to heat up in the […]
full_text: Dec 24, 2025; Honolulu, HI, USA; Hawaii Rainbow Warriors place kicker Kansei Matsuzawa (17) kicks an extra point over the California Golden Bears during the second quarter at the Hawaii Bowl at the Clarence T.C. Ching Athletics Complex. Mandatory Credit: Marco Garcia-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect A proven grizzled veteran versus a trailblazing Japanese-born undrafted rookie. That’s the high-level tale of the tape between Matt Gay and Kansei Matsuzawa, the two engaged in a kicker competition for the Las Vegas Raiders this offseason and the fight for place kicker duties and a roster spot is slated to heat up in the desert heat as training camp proceeds and preseason tilts are on tap starting next week. While plenty of attention is on head coach Klint Kubiak and his offense and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard and his defense, special teams coordinator Joe DeCamillis has quite the task himself. The competition for the starting kicker gig is chief among them, then there’s the oft-forgotten long snapper spot, and return duties, on top of that. But let’s focus on place kicker. It’s a topic I explored in early May, highlighting why the battle is an important one . “Yes, I would,” DeCamillis answered when asked if Matsuzawa is pushing Gay. “Yeah, I mean I think it’s a legitimate competition.” Gay has the edge in terms of familiarity and NFL experience. The 32-year-old Utah product is in his eighth season in the league and was DeCamillis’ kicker for the Los Angeles Rams in 2021 and 2022 — the two best years in Gay’s career where Utah native sported 94.1 and 93.3 field goal percentages missing just four field goals in that two year span. Raiders general manager John Spytek knows a bit about the 6-foot and 232 pound kicker as he served as the Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ director of player personnel during the 2019 offseason when the team drafted Gay in the fifth round (145th overall) of the 2019 NFL Draft. Gay lasted just that one season in Tampa before landing in Los Angeles. Matt Gay's two best seasons arrived in 2021 and 2022 with Joe DeCamillis as special teams boss with the Rams. Trying to recapture those 2 years where Gay was 94.1 and 93.3 percent in field goals (32-of-34 & 28-of-30). #Raiders #RaiderNation https://t.co/usCH2a5EKS — Ray Aspuria (@AsukalAspuria) March 10, 2026 Matsuzawa, meanwhile, has one of the dopest monikers in the league: “Tokyo Toe”. He’s an older undrafted free agent at 27 years old and had a stellar 2025 season at Hawaii with a 93.1 field goal percentage going 27-of-29 on his boots for the Rainbow Warriors. He finished his two-year stint at the University of Hawaii setting a school record 86.7 field goal percentage, breaking the mark held by old-school Raiders nemesis Jason Elam. A self-taught kicker via YouTube, Matsuzawa’s interest in the NFL began when sitting inside the coliseum in Oakland to watch the 2018 matchup between the Raiders and Rams. Distinct Differences As mentioned above, Gay is the seasoned vet with 102 regular season games and six playoff tilts so he’s accustomed to the high-pressure situations shouldered upon NFL kickers. In those six postseason games, Gay was 12-of-14 on field goals and 15-for-15 on extra points. Most of that came from the Rams’ 2021 Super Bowl run which harkens back to Gay having his best performances with a creative play caller in Rams head coach Sean McVay running an offense and a quality special teams boss in DeCamillis. “Yeah, he’s been hitting the ball really well. Today, obviously we had a two-minute, it was a longer field goal. One of my biggest things that I like to say is, ‘Closer is better.’ We had a lot of penalties in that two-minute period and backed him up, and we didn’t hit the ball we needed to hit right there,” DeCamillis said after one of the Raiders training camp practice sessions when asked how Gay has grown since their Las Vegas reunion. “So, we’d like to get that one over. But other than that, I mean he’s had a great offseason, a great camp so far. We’ve just got to keep him in the right groove and hopefully get him back to where he was when I had him in LA.” After a the 2022 season, Gay ended up with the Indianapolis Colts for the 2023 and 2024 seasons and spent last season between the Washington Commanders and San Francisco 49ers. The magic he once had with DeCamillis waned severely as his accuracy waned to 80.5, 83.8, 73.9, 68.4 percent before hitting all four field goal attempts with the Niners. Once known for a powerful and accurate leg (a career-long of 59 yards in 2022), Gay’s scattershot ways — he’s 48.3 percent from distances of 50-plus yards the last three seasons — must change quick if he’s going to be the one who replaces former Raiders kicker Daniel Carlson (who also experienced a sharp decline in accuracy). Then, there’s the Tokyo Toe. Las Vegas Raiders Kicker Kansei Matsuzawa Consistency is KING in Football #raiders #raidernation #LasVegasRaiders #nfl #lasvegasraidersonsi pic.twitter.com/svNmP4Jb3t — Hondo Carpenter (@HondoCarpenter) August 3, 2026 Before a sharp 2025 senior year at Hawaii, Matsuzawa went 12-of-16 in 2024. Thus his final season in college showed marked improvement. The 6-foot-2 and 200-pound kicker is an accurate specialist accustomed to volume and pressure situations as he set a school record with 27 consecutive field goals made in 2025. From short to medium range, Matsuzawa was dialed in drilling the ball through the goal posts consistently. Where’s he’s unproven, unlike Gay, is long-range ability. Hawaii didn’t attempt many field goals with the Tokyo Toe — Matsuzawa only attempted two kicks from 50 yards or more in his two seasons with the Rainbow Warriors. He made one of them: A 52-yarder against Fresno State. To capture the starting job, Gay and Matsuzawa must showcase who the most accurate, consistent, and can bang the ball through the uprights from long distance during practices and preseason games. Gay has an early lead but Matsuzawa isn’t trailing far behind. Despite the competition, both kickers are helping one another and Gay himself says Matsuzawa is “awesome” and being farther ahead as a rookie than he was back in 2019. “We get along really, really nice. He’s definitely hit the ball really well, so obviously, yeah, pushes me to keep hitting the ball well,” Gay said. “Can’t take days off and things like that. He’s awesome. I like Kansei a lot.” Who I Think Wins I believe my draft profile on Matsuzawa back in early April is a giveaway. A younger ascending option that showcased determination, accuracy and consistency to go from self taught, to Hawaii’s kicker and setting school records, and landing on an 90-man roster for an NFL team, Matsuzawa doesn’t seem the type to let this incredible opportunity slip between his fingers. With both Gay and Matsuzawa showcasing consistency and trading missed attempts during practices, the Tokyo Toe displaying in preseason games what he did for Hawaii will go a long way to separating himself from the veteran. Matsuzawa’s accuracy will also be an asset on kickoffs as he has the directional and touch skillsets that are now more apt than pure power with the league’s changed rules. And for updates on the most important battles in camp: Matt Gay is the first-team kicker, was perfect today. Kansei Matsuzawa doinked one off the right upright from 40 yards but made everything else. Tyler Duzansky is the first team long snapper. https://t.co/xYyaA2SZYl — Sam Warren (@samwarren83) July 31, 2026 If Matsuzawa is unable to claim the job, there’s still potential to make the Raiders roster as a practice squad exemption member due qualifying for the NFL’s International Player Pathway program member being born in Japan. Sort of like a stash and develop situation that Laki Tasi was in before Las Vegas waived him. “To get a roster spot for Kansei, he’s in the competition, so he’s got to do a great job there. But the great thing about his situation is, in the international part of it, there might be…

title: Raiders Mailbag: If Kirk Cousins gets injured, is Fernando Mendoza or Aidan O’Connell next man up?
summary: The pads are on, and Friday’s practice included the first fight of Las Vegas Raiders training camp, so things are certainly heating up in Southern Nevada! We have a lot to go over for this week’s mailbag, so let’s get to it! MichaelMatto I’m all in on FM sitting for a good portion or all […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JULY 29: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders looks to pass during the first practice of the team's training camp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images The pads are on, and Friday’s practice included the first fight of Las Vegas Raiders training camp , so things are certainly heating up in Southern Nevada! We have a lot to go over for this week’s mailbag, so let’s get to it! MichaelMatto I’m all in on FM sitting for a good portion or all of the season. But Kirk is an old man. I haven’t heard a peep about AOC to this point… any sense of the plan if Kirk goes down 1. during a game, or 2. for a number of games? Is FM or AOC next man up, or will that be decided at the end of camp? (If you don’t want to predict, what do you think should happen?) A: It will be interesting to see how the coaching staff stacks the quarterbacks on the depth chart, and it definitely seems like Aidan O’Connell isn’t standing out during training camp since there hasn’t been much information or reports on him so far. To be fair, that could also be a result of more eyes and attention being on Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza since those two are the main stars of the quarterback room right now. Luckily, next week’s preseason game will give O’Connell an opportunity to show people (and other teams around the league) what he’s got. The plan B behind center is something I’ve been thinking about a lot recently. To be clear, I don’t have an insight into what Klint Kubiak is thinking, but I do have a theory on what Kubiak’s plan could be. Of course, this assumes O’Connell is still on the roster for the regular season. I could see a situation where O’Connell actually begins the year as the backup/second-stringer and Mendoza is the emergency game day quarterback. Before you freak out and head to the comments section to tell me what an idiot I am, hear me out for a second! If the reason for sitting Mendoza is so that he doesn’t get thrown into the fire before he’s ready and ruin his confidence, then it would make more sense for AOC to be the backup because he’d be the one to go in the game if Cousins gets injured rather than the rookie getting thrown into a chaotic situation. But if it’s the other way around, then Mendoza’s first regular-season appearance is coming off the bench cold and having to play in a game that he didn’t get to prepare for as the starter. If Cousins is going to be out for multiple games, Kubiak can evaluate if he wants Mendoza to be the starter. In that situation, the No. 1 pick’s first regular-season appearance will be a much more controlled environment where the coaching staff can include him in the game plan, and he can prepare all week to be the starter. Neither situation is ideal, but one is a lot less chaotic than the other. Ultimately, it depends on how ready Kubiak and Co. feel Mendoza is. If they think the No. 1 pick can handle a situation where he comes off the bench cold, then without question he’ll be the Plan B. That’s similar to how Justin Herbert made his first NFL start, as the Los Angeles Chargers’ team doctor infamously punctured Tyrod Taylor’s lung while trying to give Taylor an injection for his injured ribs. That was in Week 2 of Herbert’s rookie season, and he handled the situation well and has been the Chargers’ starting quarterback ever since. However, if Kubiak wants to keep the training wheels on Mendoza, then that’s where keeping O’Connell around comes in handy so that the rookie doesn’t have to get thrown into the fire if he isn’t ready. Q: With Kirk Cousins’ history of taking his offensive weapons to Tampa for private film sessions with Jon Gruden to build chemistry, did you hear any rumblings of him doing that this summer with Fernando Mendoza, the receivers and the tight ends? A: Cousins did that after he signed with the Atlanta Falcons, and he talked about having film sessions with Mendoza during the rookie’s pre-draft visit. Also, there have been a lot of reports from OTAs, minicamp and training camp that mention those two have basically been side by side and working together a lot. So, there’s definitely some of that going on between the quarterbacks. But I haven’t heard anything about them meeting with Chucky and bringing the pass catchers down to Tampa. AAAA54 Let’s make two assumptions–that Cousins starts all 17 games and the Raiders are competing for a playoff spot the last weekend of the season. What type of season stats might we expect Cousins to put up as far as attempts, completion %, yards, TDs, INTs, sacks taken, etc. A: There are some lofty expectations here, but let’s go for it! If I had to guess, it’d probably be something like Cousins’ 2020 season, when Klint was the Vikings’ quarterbacks coach and Gary Kubiak was the offensive coordinator. Minnesota finished 7-9 that year with Cousins completing 346 passes on 516 attempts (67.6%) for 4,265 yards, 35 touchdowns and 13 interceptions . Granted, the touchdown figure is his career high, and he hasn’t thrown more than 500 passes since 2022. So, he’d probably be closer to the 25-30 touchdown mark and under 4,000 yards if the Raiders are a fringe playoff team. Q: Instead of being studs and duds, which Raider players have been pleasant surprises so far during training camp? A: The top two candidates have to be cornerback Hezekiah Masses and wide receiver Malik Benson. Despite being day three picks, both guys have been standouts during camp and appear to be pushing for a starting spot. It feels like we’ve gotten positive reports from Masses and Benson in every practice so far. Not far behind them would be a 2025 day-three guy, defensive tackle Tonka Hemingway. Reportedly, Hemingway spent a bunch of much-needed time in the weight room and keeps popping up in the one-on-ones and full team periods. RaiderEddieInDenver Hey Matt, how significant is offseason conditioning and weight room training for young lineman? Could you speak on Hemingway (I heard he’s been putting time in weight room and that it’s making a difference) and JPJ (I heard he could clean up his conditioning)? A: Putting in work in the weight room and conditioning during the offseason is more important for linemen than any other position because you’re trying to move another large human being or hold your ground against a large human being every play about 60 times a game. So, you better be strong, and you better be in shape to hold up for all four quarters. Also, while you can get some field work in as a lineman, it’s not like the skill positions where a quarterback and wide receiver can do things like routes on air or 7-on-7 that are closely related to what they’ll have to do on gamedays. The body needs a break after spending five months getting beaten up, so it’s not like you’ll see NFL linemen putting pads on and hitting each other in the trenches very often during the offseason. Plus, field work or doing position-specific drills is another form of conditioning for linemen anyway. With Hemingway, he was really athletic (for a defensive tackle) and a decent pass-rusher coming out of South Carolina and showed flashes of that during his limited snaps last season. However, Hemmingway was a questionable run defender as a prospect and really struggled in that department in year one because he wasn’t big and strong enough. At 285 pounds, he was a bit of a tweener size-wise. A little too big and not quite athletic enough to be an end but on the smaller size to play on the interior. So, Hemingway’s goal this offseason should have been to add some size and strength to become a more complete defensive tackle, and it sounds like he took that to heart. With Jackson Powers-Johnson, I think he was a good athlete for how big he was coming out of Oregon, weighing 328 pounds at the NFL Combine. That’s part of the reason he was getting some first-round buzz as a prospect and…

title: Raiders News: Maxx Crosby, Kirk Cousins get into training camp scuffle
summary: It took about two weeks, but the Las Vegas Raiders had their first training camp fight during Friday’s practice, with quarterback Kirk Cousins and defensive end Maxx Crosby getting into an altercation toward the end of the session. The Athletic’s Sam Warren detailed how the scuffle came to be, while also noting that no punches […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JUNE 09: Maxx Crosby #98 and Kirk Cousins #8 of the Las Vegas Raiders embrace during mandatory minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on June 09, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Louis Grasse/Getty Images) | Getty Images It took about two weeks, but the Las Vegas Raiders had their first training camp fight during Friday’s practice, with quarterback Kirk Cousins and defensive end Maxx Crosby getting into an altercation toward the end of the session. The Athletic’s Sam Warren detailed how the scuffle came to be, while also noting that no punches were thrown and both players were separated quickly. “The altercation came as the Raiders lined up for a final team period,” Warren wrote. “Crosby, who’d been dominant all day, burst off the line to beat Cousins’ protection. Cousins saw Crosby coming and attempted to get the ball out to rookie receiver Malik Benson on a crossing route. But Crosby got his hand up at Cousins’ release point, tipped it and forced the ball to fall short of the intended target. “Crosby stayed off Cousins’ body, complying with team rules against contacting the quarterback, although he did appear to hit the quarterback’s hand. Crosby had been physical with offensive players earlier in the day and during past practices. Cousins apparently saw this as an opportunity to stick up for his teammates.” It was also reported that the quarterback threw two interceptions—before bouncing back with a good two-minute drill period—prior to the altercation. So, maybe there was some pent-up aggression at play here. Head coach Klint Kubiak was asked about the situation between Cousins and Crosby, and Kubiak acknowledged that those two need to be smarter while brushing it off as a minor issue. “That’s training camp,” the coach said. “Those are two leaders of our team going at it, so that is part of camp. Obviously, if you fight in the game, you throw a punch in the game especially, you’re out of the game. So, we’ve got to be smart and treat it like a game.” However, this exchange wasn’t the only tussle on Friday. Warren also reported that guard Caleb Rogers and defensive lineman Jonah Laulu got into it, with Rogers grabbing Laulu and the latter throwing a punch. According to Warren, that was also broken up quickly. Kubiak was not asked about that situation specifically, but tight end Michael Mayer was available to the media after practice and shared his thoughts on the scuffles. “It’s energy, man,” Mayer said. “It’s energy. We don’t want to be throwing punches, but I think on any padded day of camp, there’s going to be some tussles. That’s our starting quarterback right now, and you want him to defend your team, and you want him to have some edge to him, which he does. He always has since the first day I met him when he came in here. So, I don’t want him getting thrown out. I don’t want him getting a flag, nothing like that. But you’ve got to be able to defend yourself.” So, it sounds like the combination of the Las Vegas heat and the first week of pads raised some tensions on Friday morning. In Other Raiders’ Links: OL/DL notes: S&BP’s Marcus Johnson was also in attendance on Friday and shared some notes about the trenches on his X/Twitter account . One highlight: “JJ Pegues looked explosive, probably the most surprising player for me during the day.” Breakout candidates: “Hemingway is an ultra athlete, he’s able to consistently use his first step and second step moves to get upfield and get past the offensive line,” S&BP’s Tristen Kuhn wrote. “…There’s issues as a run defender, where Hemingway has never been good stemming back to South Carolina, but the Raiders should put him in a spot to be a capable pass rusher.” Big day for Jack Bech: Warren noted that the wide receiver, who has been a hot topic of discussion during the early stages of training camp, had a pair of touchdowns during 1-on-1s . Is sitting Fernando Mendoza the right move?: S&BP’s newest writer, Phil Robinson, explores the topic using minority owner Tom Brady as an example .

In our weekly poll asking for fan confidence in the direction of the team, Dolphins fans averaged a 26 percent positive rating. The high-mark of the year came in Week 15, when 65 percent of the responses indicated a positive reaction […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - AUGUST 08: Miami Dolphins running back De'Von Achane (28) takes a rest during the Miami Dolphins training camp on Saturday, August 8, 2026 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, FL (Photo by Peter Joneleit/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images During the 2025 NFL season, Miami Dolphins fans had little hope for the team. In our weekly poll asking for fan confidence in the direction of the team, Dolphins fans averaged a 26 percent positive rating. The high-mark of the year came in Week 15, when 65 percent of the responses indicated a positive reaction to the direction of the team – but there were four weeks during the year when the percentage of positive votes failed to reached the double-digit mark. At the end of the year, only 15 percent of the fans were positive about the direction of the club. With the Dolphins well into their 2026 training camp and the first preseason game looming on Friday, we decided it was time to get another look at the fan confidence mark. After an offseason of change, from the President of the team down through the front office, coaching staff, and player roster, everything seems to be in a reset for the Dolphins this year. And, the fans seem to appreciate it. Even with Miami the least likely AFC team to make the playoffs this year according to the oddsmakers at FanDuel Sportsbook, the fans overwhelmingly see the Dolphins as headed in the right direction. Our training camp fan confidence poll came back with 80 percent of you feeling positively about the direction of the team. Do you agree with the poll results? How are you feeling about Miami’s direction as they prepare for their first preseason game? Head to the comments to let us know.

title: Vikings Training Camp Notes: 8/8 Edition
summary: The Minnesota Vikings took to the field again today in shells and shorts for another training camp practice at TCO Performance Center. It was hotter and sunnier than yesterday and the pace of practice was a bit slower. There was more special teams work early and another install period later in practice which also slowed […]
full_text: The Minnesota Vikings took to the field again today in shells and shorts for another training camp practice at TCO Performance Center. It was hotter and sunnier than yesterday and the pace of practice was a bit slower. There was more special teams work early and another install period later in practice which also slowed things down. So let’s get into it. Quarterback Competition This is probably the point to remind everyone that the Vikings defense allowed the second-fewest passing yards and touchdowns last year, and the passing defense ranked third overall in DVOA. I mention that now because in the competition between Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy today, the defense won. Neither quarterback completed anything particularly impressive today. Most completions (and attempts) have been short- under ten yards- and routine throws. And with a relatively few exceptions, that’s really been the case since the start of training camp. Murray has the only successful over-the-top throws against the defense- both against the first-team defense- in Wednesday’s full-pad practice. Murray had a nice deep back-shoulder pass to Jauan Jennings at the sideline today, but Jennings was unable to keep his feet in bounds- but was in position to do so- in team drills. Murray had another deep attempt to Jefferson during team drills where he might have been sacked- it was close- but the throw fell incomplete. It was a couple yards ahead of Jefferson but Murphy got flagged for either a DPI or holding call. So probably not a bad pass by Murray if he got it off in time, given the penalty on Murphy. Murray also had an intermediate pass broken up by Charles Demmings (see below). One other point of interest in today’s practice was that Murray and Justin Jefferson, together with Kevin O’Connell, were trying to sync a back shoulder throw. The first attempt happened in a red zone drill and didn’t connect, which led to O’Connell getting involved and some conversation between Murray and Jefferson after the play. The red zone drill had ended, but Murray and Jefferson tried the same play one more time and connected. But later, in team drills, Murray once again targeted Jefferson on a back shoulder throw which Jefferson got a hand on but was unable to catch. It was difficult to tell if it was Murray’s pass that was a bit off or if Jefferson took an extra step in his route before coming back for the ball, but it didn’t connect. Jefferson was upset that he didn’t make the catch after the play, so perhaps it was on Jefferson. Anyway, that is something Murray and Jefferson are working on as part of developing a rapport during training camp. For McCarthy in 11-on-11 team drills, he had one attempt in which he scrambled and may have been sacked but threw down the field to Tai Felton, who made the catch though the ball was low. However, a flag on the play negated it. He had another attempt to Felton- roughly 15 yards- that was broken up by Charles Demmings. I couldn’t tell if ball placement was an issue or not, but Demmings looked to have pretty tight coverage. Other than that, there really wasn’t anything beyond short passes from McCarthy today, and not all of those connected either. It’s fair to credit Murray for making more attempts downfield in 11-on-11 team drills, even though they didn’t connect for one reason or another, but overall credit the Vikings’ defense for making it difficult for either quarterback to connect on anything but short passes. There was also two periods of install today, with Murray working with the first team receivers on screen passes, and another where McCarthy mostly stood around while O’Connell was coaching receivers on route patterns. Other 11-on-11 Team Drill Notes Charles Demmings had 2-3 more pass break ups today, continues to shine. Chuck Demmings is something else 😂 (Via Vikings IG) pic.twitter.com/8OVdrAQZKy — VikingzFanPage (@vikingzfanpage) August 8, 2026 Demond Claiborne had an impressive jump cut after coming right up to the back of his offensive lineman, jumping over one gap and instantly accelerating through the hole for what I think may have been a genuine touchdown run if he was able to break a safety tackle. Demond Claiborne ⚡️ (Via Vikings IG) https://t.co/v7EPc454OX pic.twitter.com/bcULxWlYJw — VikingzFanPage (@vikingzfanpage) August 9, 2026 Domonique Orange ‘Big Citrus’ had a nice penetration for a TFL I did not see Levi Drake-Rodriguez at practice today, both initially for stretching or in team drills. Not sure why. Brian O’Neill also did not participate although he was there in uniform with a baseball hat on. Probably just a day off for him. Defensive tackle Eric Johnson II tipped a McCarthy pass on a scramble. Of the longer-shot defensive tackles to make the roster, he may be toward the top of the list. Eric Wilson had another would-be sack on McCarthy today and was playing some edge rusher. It doesn’t appear that Wilson, based on who is participating in special teams drills, will have much of a role on special teams this year after being a core special teamer last year. From Matt Daniels’ press conferences, it appears that he is counting on Ivan Pace Jr. to be a leader on special teams. He’s mentioned this in two press conferences now, which would seem to indicate he has a roster spot. That has seemed very much in doubt after the additions of Jake Golday and Jamal Adams, but it appears the Vikings want him as a core special teamer. Defensive tackle Elijah Williams has been getting regular rotation with both first and second team defenses and had nice stop today on a Jordan Mason run. Tai Felton took over for Jordan Addison on the first-team offense with Addison still nursing a stubbed finger. Addison did catch some balls in drills, however, suggesting he is near to returning to full-go. That’s all I have for today. Tomorrow is the Vikings’ night practice, which I will not be able to attend. I will return to Vikings’ training camp next week. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

title: Sunday Patriots Notes: Under-the-radar players starting to emerge in training camp
summary: The dog days of summer have arrived in Foxborough. The New England Patriots took the practice fields on five straight days between Monday and Friday, including four times in full pads. The rhythm of this year’s training camp is going to change next week, with a joint practice and first game on the schedule. For […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 01: New England Patriots linebacker Khalil Jacobs (59) participate in drills during training camp on August 1, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, MA. (Photo by M. Anthony Nesmith/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The dog days of summer have arrived in Foxborough. The New England Patriots took the practice fields on five straight days between Monday and Friday, including four times in full pads. The rhythm of this year’s training camp is going to change next week, with a joint practice and first game on the schedule. For now, however, let’s put a wrap on the week that was. Welcome to the latest addition of our Sunday Patriots Notes . Under-the-radar players starting to emerge in training camp Training camp is not just the time for a team to forge its identity before the regular season, it also is an opportunity for players to make a name for themselves regardless of their background. The Patriots have seen multiple of those starting to emerge over the last few days. The obvious one is Tanner Arkin, an undrafted rookie who looks like the Patriots’ best blocking tight end and is on track to making the roster. Other notables are edge defender Xavier Holmes, who has had some flashes of disruptive play, as well as well as cornerbacks Karon Prunty and Channing Canada; both of the rookies are in contention for the fifth and sixth spots on the depth chart. Among the more veteran players, Marcus Bryant emerging as the top backup left tackle was a surprising development considering the presence of first-round draft pick Caleb Lomu. The same can be said for third-year man Terrell Jennings immediately resuming the RB3 role upon his return from the non-football injury list. The most notable development relative to his starting point, however, might belong to Khalil Jacobs. The undrafted rookie, who wasn’t even part of the first wave of signings, appears well-positioned to make the roster as a fourth off-ball linebacker. “He loves football,” said head coach Mike Vrabel about the 22-year-old. “He’s here a lot. He was here in the offseason, through the minicamps, early, staying late. He stays late. I see him here all the time.” Besides his work ethic, Jacobs also caught the eye due to his speed — a topic of discussion going all the way back to his pre-draft visit with the club. “When you get to the team periods, you notice his play speed, and I think that’s a great thing to say,” Vrabel added. “He came here on a visit, and I was trying to just give him a hard time about his 40, and he was like, ‘Oh, that was the timing.’ I’m like, ‘Thirty-two teams timed your 40 wrong?’ Just giving him a hard time. But to his credit, he plays a lot faster than whatever his 40 was. … He has a play speed about him, and sometimes he knows where he’s going, and sometimes he doesn’t, but he still kind of goes pretty quick wherever he decides to go.” For Jacobs, the speed element is important regardless of the 4.77-seconds he posted in the 40-yard dash during the draft process. “The math wasn’t mathing,” he said. “We play football, we’re not track runners. I have tremendous game speed, so I won’t allow 40 times and things like that determine the kind of player I am. … I play extremely fast. Once I see ball, get ball. I try not to think so much, allowing myself to go make plays, and try to make myself be in positions where I can make those plays.” So far this training camp, Jacobs has made his fair share of plays. It has allowed him to establish himself as a fourth linebacker behind Robert Spillane, Christian Elliss and Chad Muma. And if his journey so far is any indication, he is not intent on giving it up. “When my opportunity came, I just made the most of it,” he said. “I didn’t look back.” Upward trajectory Even though he has missed reps due to an apparent left arm injury, Will Campbell was off to a strong start this summer. His teammates noticed it too. “Will has definitely gotten better from the last time I played him last year,” said offseason signing Dre’Mont Jones. “He’s definitely watched a lot of film and honed in his technique even more. It’s fun to watch and it’s fun to compete against him every day.” “He just gets it,” added quarterback Drake Maye. “He gets how to practice, having to come here and show up every day because there are no days off. In practice and in this league, when you’re blocking guys in 1-on-1s, and you’ve got team next, and then we have two-minute. It’s constant, and I think that’s what Will is understanding: how it’s different from college. It’s constant, and you’ve got to train your body and train your mind to be out here each and every day, and treat it like, ‘Man, I’ve got to try to get better today.’ I think he’s learned that really fast, and I think he’s taking it head on, and I’m looking forward to seeing him this year do his thing.” Mike Vrabel indicated on Friday that Campbell should be able to up his workload this coming week. Summer camp vibes When the Patriots drafted teams for their scrimmage on Friday, there were only two rules. The first was that Drake Maye and Jared Wilson had to stay together, an unsurprising decision considering the importance of the quarterback-center relationship. The second was that Mack Hollins and Efton Chism also needed to be on the same team, an unsurprising decision considering the importance of bromance. “It’s unbelievable. You come in there, and they’re in the pool, the rehab pool, and they’re playing like pool games,” said Mike Vrabel about Hollins and Chism. “It’s like summer camp. They’re throwing stuff and got goggles on, and they swim down and pick up things on the bottom of the pool. They study all the time. They work out. They train. They compete. They push each other.” Hollins and Chism both arrived in New England last offseason. The former joined the team as a veteran free agency signing, the latter as an undrafted rookie. “It’s a really cool thing to see,” added Vrabel. “A guy that had been in this league a long time, played with a couple different teams and a kid from Western Washington, a small school, and they come together, and I think they both help each other.” List of 2023 first-round pick extensions keeps growing While the Patriots and Christian Gonzalez still await a conclusion to their own contract extension saga, multiple other 2023 first-round draft picks have signed new deals of their own. Including Titans guard Peter Skoronski, who just signed a reported four-year, $100 million extension before the weekend, the list now looks like this: ED Will Anderson Jr. (1-3): 3 years, $150M RB Bijan Robinson (1-8): 3 years, $66.75M DT Jalen Carter (1-9): 4 years, $152M OT Darnell Wright (1-10): 4 years, $116M (reported) OL Peter Skoronski (1-11): 4 years, $100M (reported) RB Jahmyr Gibbs (1-12): 3 years, $67.5M LB Jack Campbell (1-18): 4 years, $81M WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba (1-20): 4 years, $168.6M WR Zay Flowers (1-22): 4 years, $140M What stands out is that none of the four cornerbacks selected in the first round in 2023, including Gonzalez, have been extended. The big name to watch in that regard is Seattle’s Devon Witherspoon, drafted fifth overall. He very well could become the first domino to drop. Versatility is key The competition for the third safety spot is seemingly down to incumbent Dell Pettus and free agency signing Mike Brown, with both getting starer reps throughout the summer. For Pettus, who appears to have taken a slight lead over the last week, the secret to winning is simply being able to do whatever is asked of him. “I’m just trying to continue to be consistent and continue to prove to the staff that I can wear many hats and also do one as equally as the other,” he explained. “Playing safety the same way, playing nickel, dime. Wherever they put me, I’m going to play it to my fullest potential no matter what. I just want them to be able to trust me and build confidence that no matter where they put me at, that I will…

title: Mike Vrabel recalls his favorite Adam Vinatieri story
summary: Adam Vinatieri officially enters the Pro Football Hall of Fame on Saturday, becoming the latest member of the New England Patriots dynasty to receive the highest individual honor in the game. It is not hard to see why: his career includes game-winning field goals in two of the organization’s Super Bowl win as well as […]
full_text: UNITED STATES - SEPTEMBER 25: Football: Closeup of New England Patriots Adam Vinatieri (4) victorious after making game winning field goal kick vs Pittsburgh Steelers, Pittsburgh, PA 9/25/2005 (Photo by Fred Vuich/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (SetNumber: X74303 TK2) Adam Vinatieri officially enters the Pro Football Hall of Fame on Saturday, becoming the latest member of the New England Patriots dynasty to receive the highest individual honor in the game. It is not hard to see why: his career includes game-winning field goals in two of the organization’s Super Bowl win as well as multiple other legendary moments and NFL records. It also includes a story about a sports car purchase gone wrong. Let current Patriots coach and Vinatieri’s former teammate Mike Vrabel explain. “I think the favorite story is he showed up one offseason with a yellow Lamborghini or Ferrari or something, and we crushed him,” he recalled. “I think he took it back and then got a normal color.” The sports car story was not the only one Vrabel mentioned when asked about Vinatieri on Friday, however. He also spoke about arguably the best kick in NFL history, a 45-yard field goal in blizzard conditions to tie the Patriots’ 2001 divisional playoff game against the Raiders at 13-13. “The kick in the snow, if you were there, you were on that field, to be able to think that could somehow be done. I struggled to run on that field that day, and he was able to make the kick that he made,” Vrabel said. “It was always just – any time we got into those situations, we knew if we can just get it to the 35-yard line that we were going to win the football game. And so, for him to be able to do that in the biggest moments was a pleasure. He trained hard, he had a routine, engaged with. He wasn’t off. He wasn’t the lonely kicker, wasn’t by himself. He was a part of the football team.” Vinatieri was part of the Patriots for the first 10 seasons of his 24-year career in the NFL. On Saturday, he will join another club: that of the Pro Football Hall of Famers, and deservedly so.

The moment @adamvinatieri 's bust was revealed 🙌 pic.twitter.com/uS1OgQxuBp — New England Patriots (@Patriots) August 8, 2026 An undrafted free agent out of South Dakota State, Vinatieri arrived in New England in 1996. He spent the first 10 seasons of his 24-year NFL career with the Patriots, and was a cornerstone of their first three championship teams. He kicked game-winning field goals in two of those Super Bowl wins, and additionally made arguably the best kick in NFL history when he split the uprights from 45 yards out in a 2001 divisional round win over the Oakland Raiders. Vinatieri, who finished his legendary career with a 14-year stint in Indianapolis, made 83.8% of his regular season field goals as well as 81.2% in the playoffs. Arguably the most clutch kicker the league has ever seen, he retired as a four-time Super Bowl winner, three-time All-Pro selection, one-time All-Decade selection (2000s) and the owner of multiple NFL records, including points scored in a career (2,673) The now-53-year-old was later also named to the league’s 100th Anniversary Team. On Saturday, he earned the famous golden jacket alongside fellow pro football legends Drew Brees, Roger Craig, Larry Fitzgerald and Luke Kuechly.

title: Why Adam Vinatieri entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame on Saturday
summary: The Pro Football Hall of Fame came under significant scrutiny this February after its 50 voters decided against both the most successful head coach and the most successful owner in NFL history. As bad as the Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft decisions were, the consortium did get one right: making Adam Vinatieri a Hall of […]
full_text: The Pro Football Hall of Fame came under significant scrutiny this February after its 50 voters decided against both the most successful head coach and the most successful owner in NFL history. As bad as the Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft decisions were, the consortium did get one right: making Adam Vinatieri a Hall of Famer. After being denied in his first year of eligibility in 2025, Vinatieri garnered enough votes to make it in this year. He will do so alongside quarterback Drew Brees, running back Roger Craig, wide receiver Larry Fitzgerald and linebacker Luke Kuechly. It is an honor Vinatieri has definitely earned. Why Adam Vinatieri is a Pro Football Hall of Famer Championship pedigree: In theory — one that is being tested especially in light of the aforementioned Belichick decision — the Hall of Fame has a simple purpose. It exists to honor and preserve the game’s history by recognizing the best and most influential players, coaches and contributors in the game; the men (and, yes, it’s exclusively men) who shaped the sport into what it is today. Arguably not just the greatest and most recognizable, but also the most valuable kicker in league history, Vinatieri is one of those people. The value he provided to pro football can be measured in Super Bowl rings, of which he has four, and also via his contributions to literally kickstarting the Patriots’ two-decade dynasty. Without him nailing three overtime game winners during the 2001 season, arguably the best kick the league has ever seen, and the walk-off field goal in Super Bowl XXXVI, who knows what New England’s unprecedented run of success would have looked like. Highlight-reel moments: There may not be another kicker in NFL history, and frankly, few players overall, with as jam-packed a highlight reel as Vinatieri’s. The game winners are only a fraction of the massive plays he made over the course of his 24-year career. Vinatieri made crucial kicks in the first three of the Patriots’ six Super Bowls victories so far, including last-second winners in two of those. He also had a five-field goal performance in a 15-6 divisional round victory to pave the way for the Colts to win a championship in 2006. On top of those, he also made a massive 45-yard field goal to send the Patriots’ to overtime in the 2001 divisional round against the Raiders. Ready to feel old? Adam Vinatieri kicked the #Patriots to a 16-13 divisional-round playoff win over the Raiders in the Snow Bowl … 21 years ago today. pic.twitter.com/FiVRpqgkvs — Andrew Callahan (@_AndrewCallahan) January 19, 2023 That kick, as mentioned above, has a case as the best pro football has ever seen. And yet, in Vinatieri’s storied career it is one of many standout plays. Longevity: As mentioned by NFLPA interim executive director David White ahead of the Super Bowl, the average NFL career lasts between three and four years. That number is slightly higher for kickers given the less demanding nature of the position, but reaching Vinatieri’s spheres is still a rarity even at that spot: an undrafted free agent in 1996, he remained in the league until 2019. His 24 total seasons rank third all-time behind only fellow Hall of Famers George Blanda (26) and Morten Andersen (25). In those 24 years, Vinatieri appeared in a combined 365 regular season games and retired as the all-time leader in career field goals (599) and points scored (2,673). He also played 32 playoff games — i.e. an extra two seasons worth of postseason action under the old 16-game format — and hit 56 field goals in the tournament, another all-time mark. In addition to those numbers, Vinatieri’s four Super Bowl rings are also the most among all kickers. Those numbers alone speak a clear language already. Which kickers are in the Hall of Fame now? Until Vinatieri officially enters on Saturday, only two exclusive placekickers have found their way to Canton: Jan Stenerud in 1991, and the aforementioned Morten Andersen in 2017. Vinatieri is now the third to join them, and is the most realistic candidate at the position to receive the honor in the foreseeable future. In addition to Stenerud, Andersen and now Vinatieri, nine other players have been enshrined who have served as kickers before the era of positional specialization. All of them primarily played other positions on top of also kicking field goals and extra points: George Blanda, Lou Groza, Pete Henry, Paul Hornung, Don Hutson, Bobby Layne, Les Richter, Ken Strong, and Doak Walker. They all will be getting some much-deserved company in the Hall of Fame on Saturday.

title: 3-Point Stance: Competition is at the heart of the Patriots’ growth
summary: After a bounce-back 2026 season that saw the New England Patriots return to the Super Bowl coming off back-to-back 4-13 finishes the two years prior, internal competition is pushing the roster towards further improvement. It’s a trait that played a significant role in head coach Mike Vrabel’s playing career, and now, it’s extending into his […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 06: New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel arrives to New England Patriots training camp on August 6, 2026 at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After a bounce-back 2026 season that saw the New England Patriots return to the Super Bowl coming off back-to-back 4-13 finishes the two years prior, internal competition is pushing the roster towards further improvement. It’s a trait that played a significant role in head coach Mike Vrabel’s playing career, and now, it’s extending into his coaching philosophy as training camp progresses. On Monday, media members got a close look at that competition after heavy rain moved a previously scheduled outdoor practice inside the field bubble. Friendly banter echoed from both sides of the ball throughout team periods as each unit tried to one-up the other. And as long as that trash talk is “authentic” and doesn’t distract the players from completing their assignments on the field, Vrabel sees the competition as a team builder. “I think the competitiveness has been great,” Vrabel said on Tuesday. “I want that. I think we need that. I think that’s part of building a team, but then also the line that we take [the players] to is being able to take care of each other. We’re not throwing punches. We’re not into that … But I’m all for the energy and the trash talk and the back and forth and being able to get back and then do your job.” That competitive spirit reflects a connected team culture built on players challenging themselves and the others around them. It’s a core identity of how this team is building on their 2025 success and looking to improve. Vrabel’s fostered environment The star matchup between Christian Gonzalez and A.J. Brown has been one of the highlights of training camp. Both players regularly compete during one-on-ones and in team periods, trading friendly trash talk. However, that banter escalated on Thursday, as the two engaged in a brief face-to-face exchange following a Gonzalez pass breakup and camera-pointing gesture. Gonzalez spoke with the media after that moment, explaining there’s never personal disrespect involved; that competition is just how you get better. “I mean, it’s good on good,” Gonzalez said on Thursday . “You know, [Brown’s] a number one receiver in this league, going up against a number one corner. I mean, that’s how it’s going to go. It’s football at the end of the day. There’s never any disrespect or anything. We’re just battling and getting each other better. “He’s going to face corners like that who are going to yap at him and going to try to get in his head. And I’m going to face receivers like that who are strong and come right back at me. So it’s great work for both of us.” On Friday, Brown joked that Gonzalez’s intensity on the field increases when the two are matched up. “Every day is a battle with [Gonzalez]. It’s nothing but respect,” Brown said. “Ultimately, it’s not about me and him. We’re out here competing. All of us are challenging each other for the greater of the team.” And their head coach appreciates the battle between them, he said on Tuesday, explaining that the matchup sets the tone by sending a “clear and easy” message to the team about how they’re supposed to compete and challenge each other. “I appreciate what A.J. and Gonzo have done is just come in and compete and try to improve,” Vrabel said. “It’s been a good battle, and that’s pro football. I love watching it, and I think that there’s a great amount of respect that each of those players have for each other and understand that the work that they’re putting in now is going to pay dividends in the season.” One player who can attest to Vrabel’s embrace of player competition is Kevin Byard. The safety shared that his coach talks trash to the offense or defense when the other side is winning, which reflects Vrabel’s competitive nature. “I’ve heard plenty of stories of him being here, getting on the scout team, picking off Tom Brady and stuff like that,” Byard said on Monday. “I think he’s just a competitive guy. So he wants his team to have that same competitive spirit.” Competition is driving improvement In the defense’s battle with the offense, Byard uses those experiences to correct his mistakes and find ways to improve. That means asking offensive players about their techniques and decisions. One thing he asks Hunter Henry is about the tight end’s tendency to use both hands to push off a safety when he’s running a route and expecting press coverage. Some tight ends, according to Byard, will “throw an elbow” instead. Understanding those tendencies helps the veteran adjust his counter and leverage accordingly. He values feedback from his teammates because, unlike the coaches, the players are the ones on the field executing those assignments. “Looking at a guy like Hunter, we both came in at the same time and played a lot of ball. So you’re just learning from each other,” Byard said on Monday. “And I think it’s the same thing when I’m asking Drake like, ‘Hey, what are you seeing in these coverages?’, [or], ‘Hey, we’re disguising this. What makes you check to a different call, or what makes you motion the receiver over?’ “It’s just those small things, getting little nuances, and that’s what training camp is for … But we’re out here trying to get a good sense of what he’s looking at, what he’s seeing, and how I can try to counter off that to try to make him make a mistake because we’re all out here competing, trying to beat each other. That’s what it is.” That environment is also pushing players to set goals and find new ways to test themselves throughout training camp. Third-year safety Dell Pettus revealed on Monday that last Saturday, Byard actually challenged the secondary to create more takeaways after the defense only forced one turnover through the first six practices. And Pettus delivered, securing the unit’s second interception on Maye this summer, which is one the defense “needed.” “After those first few practices, [Byard] brought us up, and he was like, ‘We need takeaways today,’” Pettus shared on Monday. “Before we went to any competitive team activity, he said, ‘We need more takeaways; we’re going to go out here and go get the football. Forget what everybody else is talking about; forget what the coaches talk about. This is our team. This is our defensive backfield.’ … And I told him I thought that was great to hear just because he set the tone for us that day.” Fast forward to Thursday, and the defense logged three consecutive interceptions during two-minute drills against Maye and Tommy DeVito’s offenses. A family culture is building confidence Both sides of the trenches also openly communicate, pointing out “tells” or tendencies they notice of the opposite unit to help each other improve. Will Campbell believes that collaboration comes from a “tight-knit” team culture. “I think it’s the nature of the family feeling in this building,” Campbell said. “As much as we want to kick their asses in practice and they want to kick ours, we want them to get as many sacks as possible, and they want us to give up as few as possible. We’re all trying to help each other get better because that’s the way that we’re going to be successful during the season.” From defensive tackle Milton Williams’ perspective, he can consistently pick up on one or two tells every practice; however, he waits until after practice to share them so he can maintain a competitive edge. He adds that the offensive line does a “good job” of building on that feedback. “Just telling them I’m always looking at their stance,” Williams said about what those conversations are like. “Any pass or run tail that they’re giving us up front because I know other [defensive] linemen across the league are looking at the same thing … But having those conversations knowing that I’m not the only one listening to those…

The Notre Dame product was grouped with Maye on the white team. Although the squad fell short 22-15, the third-round draft selection caught back-to-back passes from his quarterback to open a two-minute drill, which set up a successful Andy Borregales field goal attempt. When asked about how the rookie was adapting to the speed of the NFL earlier this offseason, Mike Vrabel said he’d rather players make mistakes while playing fast than hesitate because of overthinking. That philosophy has helped Raridon play faster and become a more consistent contributor. “Yeah, I feel like this is kind of a new mentality coach Vrabel is installing in us, and it’s been great,” Raridon said on Friday. “It’s helping me play fast, and a lot of helping you play fast is knowing what to do on offense. That’s been getting easier for me. So, because of that mentality [and] me being able to process information, I’ve been able to play faster.” Raridon hauled in three receptions from Maye throughout the scrimmage. The first was a deep connection up the seam on a block-and-release play-action assignment that re-ignited a once stagnant offense and led to the white team’s first touchdown score. Before that gain, Maye was one of six on his passing attempts. “I feel like every day is starting to get better, and I definitely feel like I’m improving,” Raridon said about his comfort level with the playbook. “A lot of that is due to the comfortability I’m having in the offense. So, every day is getting easier because the offense is starting to seep into my brain a little bit.” The 22-year-old also credited New England’s coaching staff as a primary reason why he’s grown more acclimated to the offense. “I think a lot of it is the coaching,” Raridon added. “I’ve had really good coaches here. [Tight ends coach Thomas Brown] and coach Vrabel have done a great job of getting on me and [helping] me improve. We’re meeting a lot here [at training camp] and processing a lot of information and learning a lot. That requires me to study outside of being at the facility. So the studying has helped, the coaching I’ve been having has helped and just every day it starts to get easier.” Next week, the Patriots will host the Indianapolis Colts for a joint practice on Tuesday before Raridon is slated to make his NFL preseason debut in Thursday’s matchup between the two franchises. While the rookie is uncertain what nerves he’ll feel before the contest, Raridon said he’s going to approach it like every other game he’s played. “I’m excited to compete against other teams,” Raridon said. “It’s fun to compete against my guys, but I’m ready to take the field with them and be part of a team and compete with other teams.”

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for WR Romeo Doubs
summary: The New England Patriots passing offense enjoyed considerable success during the 2025 season, but the need for improvement became obvious during the playoffs. Going against some of the NFL’s top-tier offenses, the lack of top-tier talent became an issue that contributed to the unit’s postseason struggles. And so, the Patriots set out to fix the […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 01: New England Patriots wide receiver Romeo Doubs (87) warms up during training camp on August 1, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, MA. (Photo by M. Anthony Nesmith/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots passing offense enjoyed considerable success during the 2025 season, but the need for improvement became obvious during the playoffs. Going against some of the NFL’s top-tier offenses, the lack of top-tier talent became an issue that contributed to the unit’s postseason struggles. And so, the Patriots set out to fix the problem. One of the first investments made to do so was signing ex-Packers wideout Romeo Doubs to a four-year contract in free agency — a deal that sets him up to be one of the team’s most important receivers in 2026 and beyond. Hard facts Name: Romeo Doubs Position: Wide receiver Jersey number: 87 Opening day age: 26 (4/13/2000) Measurements : 6’1 7/8”, 204 lbs, 10” hand size, 32 1/4” arm length, 77 3/8” wingspan, 13 bench press reps, N/A Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: Green Bay Packers (2022-25), New England Patriots (2026-) | College: Nevada (2018-21) Productive in a multi-faceted role during his high school career at Jefferson in Los Angeles, Doubs was a fairly highly-regarded college recruit who ended up getting almost a dozen scholarship offers as a three-star prospect. He eventually opted for the University of Nevada, where he was a heavily-involved wide receiver from the get-go and in his 44 total games ended up catching 225 passes for 3,322 yards and 26 touchdowns. A first-team All-Mountain West selection as both a junior and senior, Doubs entered the NFL in 2022 and was selected 132nd overall in the fourth round by the Packers. Once at the pro level, he picked up right where he left off. Doubs caught 42 passes his rookie year, good enough for fourth on the team and second among its wide receivers. Since then, he only strengthened his position in the Packers offense, and by the end of his fourth season in Green Bay had a combined 63 regular season and playoff appearances as well as 222 total receptions for 2,795 yards and 23 touchdowns on his résumé. Doubs turned his Packers tenure into a four-year, $68 million free agency deal with the Patriots in 2026. Scouting report Strengths: Doubs lacks some of the athletic traits the NFL’s top-flight wide receivers possess, but he has developed into a dependable receiving target nonetheless. From the release through the stem of the route to the catch point he has become a lot more refined, while showing a good feel for leverage and defensive coverage — a mix of skills that has made him particularly effective working in the red zone. Additionally, he has been getting better as a hands catcher and in the blocking department. Doubs is more than capable of making an impact on all three downs and from all over the formation. He also is able to generate quick separation and work the underneath areas of the field against both man and zone. In short, he is as consistent a wide receiver as you will find and therefore somebody deserving of the “go-to guy” label. Weaknesses: Doubs is not the most imposing athlete both in terms of build and explosiveness. He has good length but lacks size overall, which in turn puts pressure on his technique to beat press-man coverage or win contested catches. He makes up for it with natural hands and good concentration, but he is not a 50/50 jump ball specialist you would trust in such situations on a regular basis. He also won’t consistently challenge teams deep, in part because he lacks high-end long speed and his game as a whole is more horizontal than vertical. 2025 review Stats : 17 games (16 starts) | 832 offensive snaps (74.2%), 38 special teams snaps (8.5%) | 94 targets, 63 catches (67.0%), 848 receiving yards (13.5/catch), 7 TDs, 4 drops | 15 punt returns, 94 yards (6.3/return) | 1 penalty (incl. 0 declined/offsetting) Season recap: Doubs’ 2024 season ended in disappointment when he had to leave his team’s playoff loss to Philadelphia with a concussion. He managed to bounce back strongly, however, and in the final year under his rookie contract played arguably the best football of his career. Fully establishing himself as quarterback Jordan Love’s favorite receiver and a core piece of the Packers offense, Doubs finished the regular season ranked first on the team in targets (83), receptions (55) and receiving yards (724), and was tied for the lead in touchdowns (6). His production fluctuated a bit through the year, but he shined repeatedly. Whether it was catching three touchdowns against the Cowboys, hauling in seven receptions for 91 yards versus the Panthers, or averaging 20.7 yards on three receptions versus Baltimore, Doubs combined a high volume of snaps and opportunities with big-play potential. Never became that more apparent than the postseason. Even though Green Bay ended up coming short again, Doubs was on fire in the playoffs. He caught eight passes on 11 targets for 124 yards and a touchdown in the Packers’ 31-27 wild card loss to the Bears. ROMEO DOUBS WITH ONE HAND 😳 GBvsCHI on Prime Video Also streaming on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/EyFBmRtXRf — NFL (@NFL) January 11, 2026 Doubs’ efforts in the game against the Bears ultimately were for naught, but the fourth-year receiver showed a national audience — and the rest of the NFL — what he is capable of. Less than two months later, he was cashing in because of, in part, his performance that day and throughout the 2025 campaign overall. 2026 preview Position: Z/X-receiver | Ability: Quality starter | Contract: Signed through 2029 (2030 UFA) What will be his role? As if his contract wasn’t already enough of an indication, training camp confirmed that Doubs will be a starting receiver in New England. With A.J. Brown the top option on the perimeter and DeMario Douglas holding down the fort in the slot, he projects as the primary Z-receiver but is flexible enough to move elsewhere in the formation if the personnel package or play selection call for it. Either way, he should end 2025 among the Patriots’ leaders in wide receiver snaps, targets and catches. What is his growth potential? Even though his statistical production may not suggest so, Doubs improved as a receiver every season since entering the NFL. In every facet of the game, he is a better player now than he was earlier in his career. The hope for the Patriots is that the arrow will continue pointing up in an offense led by an MVP runner-up quarterback and one of the best play-callers in football. Does he have positional versatility? Even though he is the top Z-receiver on paper, Doubs will not be confined to one particular role in the Patriots’ offense. He lines up at the Z, but is also capable of moving to X or even to the slot when the team goes to condensed looks. Naturally, catching the football is his main task but New England would not have brought him in if he couldn’t also help out as a blocker in the run game. He additionally offers some special teams experience: besides the 15 punt returns he had in 2025, he also ran back a pair of kickoffs as a rookie. What is his salary cap situation? As noted above, Doubs signed a four-year, $68 million contract with the Patriots in March. The deal comes with an $8.6 million cap figure for the 2026 season that can be broken down as follows: it consists of a base salary ($3M), signing bonus proration ($3.75M), roster bonus ($1.7M) and two workout bonus prorations ($75k + $75k) as well as incentives classified as not likely to be earned ($3M). With the logical exception of the incentives, all of those numbers are guaranteed. How safe is his roster spot? Doubs is a nailed-on lock to make the Patriots’ roster this season and play a major role in their offensive operation. The real question is just how effectively his chemistry with quarterback Drake Maye will develop, but there have been promising…

title: Saints Training Camp Week 1 Injury Update
summary: Since rebuilding their entire training staff, the New Orleans Saints have seen a positive impact on their team. Even though there were some major injuries throughout last season- that’s always going to happen in football- the pesky soft tissue issues that plagued the team in the past have not been as prevalent. This season, the […]
full_text: Since rebuilding their entire training staff, the New Orleans Saints have seen a positive impact on their team. Even though there were some major injuries throughout last season- that’s always going to happen in football- the pesky soft tissue issues that plagued the team in the past have not been as prevalent. This season, the hope was that their injury luck would continue, and although things could be worse, after Week 1, there have already been some issues that affect the roster. So, let’s look this week’s injury update for the Saints. Bryan Bresee – Out for the season (Knee) By now everybody knows about this one, but it’s important to still talk about. Bryan Bresee was set to be a major piece on the defensive line, and for his future career, it needed to be a big year from him. Instead, after suffering a knee injury, Bresee will be out for the entire season. For the Saints’ defensive line, it’s going to be harder for the Saints to deal with this loss, and for Bresee, this puts extreme pressure on him next season. It’s going to be a contract year, and if Bresee can’t bounce back and show improvement, the Saints may not bring him back. Christen Miller – Day-to-Day (Toe) Before training camp, DT Christen Miller was dealing with some injury issues, but has been healthy since. He is an extremely important piece of the defensive line, just like Bresee was, but Miller’s main spot will be at nose tackle. Miller should be the heir apparent to Davon Godchaux, and staying on the field could accelerate that. Recently, it was announced that Miller suffered a very minor toe injury, and it seems that he will be day-to-day moving forward. Kendre Miller – Day-to-Day (Back) The RB depth on the Saints roster must stay healthy to make it past cuts because the competition behind Alvin Kamara and Travis Etienne will be close. Staying healthy is probably the most important factor for Kendre Miller, who has been unable to do just that. But he is currently dealing with a minor back injury, and if he can’t return soon, it may be something the coaching staff remembers. Jeremiah Wright – Day-to-Day (Shoulder) Last on the updated injury report is guard Jeremiah Wright. Behind Cesar Ruiz, Wright has an oppurtunity to develop and be ready to step in if Ruiz gets injured or if the Saints just want to make a change. So far in training camp, Wright has been doing well and probably a bit better than many expected, but a recent shoulder injury has prevented him from participating.
