title: Survey results: Giants fans are feeling the optimism
summary: The summer is the season for optimism around the NFL, the time when fans of every team allow themselves to indulge in hope for the coming season. The New York Giants have had a bit more than a week of training camp and are about a week away from their first preseason game on August […]
full_text: Fans watch the Giants during training camp. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The summer is the season for optimism around the NFL, the time when fans of every team allow themselves to indulge in hope for the coming season. The New York Giants have had a bit more than a week of training camp and are about a week away from their first preseason game on August 15th. Rather than asking about anything specific before seeing the team on the field in a live situation, we wanted to take the temperature of the fanbase as things start to ramp up. It isn’t much of a surprise that the overwhelming majority of Giants fans are either optimistic, or outright excited, about their team. That flies in the face of the national perspective, where the Giants are an afterthought and even outright derided. Even Las Vegas views the Giants as extreme long-shots to make the playoffs this year, with the second-longest odds in the NFC, per FanDuel . We’ll see if the fans or the national perspective is right, but so far the news out of camp has been almost universally positive. Camp under John Harbaugh has been faster and tougher than what we’ve seen in recent years from the Giants, with a much higher level of accountability. The defense under Dennard Wilson has been consistently disruptive and at times dominant. The pass rush has been making the quarterbacks’ lives difficult while the secondary hasn’t been giving up much separation at all. And while they aren’t hauling in all their interception opportunities, the defensive backs seem to be playing faster and more confidently than we saw the last two years. The defense hasn’t been allowing the offense to establish much rhythm or consistency, but we’re still getting positive reports out of that side of the ball as well. Both WR Malik Nabers and RB Cam Skattebo are healthier than many of us on the outside anticipated, and Odell Beckham Jr. has been rounding into form with increased reps. Rookie WR Malachi Fields has produced highlight reel catches with regularity, and the offensive line has looked good as well — despite the pass rush consistently getting into the backfield. It seems that’s just a function of the Giants’ hyper-athletic front seven, not poor play on the part of the blockers. There are, of course, fans who aren’t drinking the Big Blue kool-aid just yet — And that’s fair. After all, the Giants looked amazing in camp and preseason last year, but still managed to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory on five separate occasions during the season. We’ll see how the good reports translate into the preseason, as well as how the Giants progress over their three preseason games. Last year there were consistent lapses in execution and assignment discipline that were never resolved and became the team’s Achilles heel in the season. Even if the Giants don’t win their preseason games, we’ll see a solid baseline of execution and what issues that crop up be corrected.

The team will travel back to their own facilities tomorrow before getting back to work in advance of facing the Minnesota Vikings in their first preseason game next weekend. title: The Giants’ first-round drafting track record through the decade
summary: The New York Giants — and our esteemed editor Ed Valentine — are at the Greenbrier Resort in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, for John Harbaugh’s first training camp as head football coach of the Giants. Mike Renner wrote a detailed article ranking and evaluating 191 first-round selections since 2020. Rather than simply ranking the […]
full_text: Andrew Thomas | Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images The New York Giants — and our esteemed editor Ed Valentine — are at the Greenbrier Resort in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, for John Harbaugh’s first training camp as head football coach of the Giants. Mike Renner wrote a detailed article ranking and evaluating 191 first-round selections since 2020. Rather than simply ranking the best players drafted in the first round from 2020-2025, Mike Renner of CBS Sports evaluated each decision from the team’s point of view and the draft slot the player was selected. It’s not just Renner ranking the players, but also the value of the pick itself. The 2026 draft was not included, but the 2020-2025 classes are, and Renner breaks down his ranking in thirds. Renner used three tiers to organize the 191 first-round selections. He then shifted to a team-by-team audit, explaining which franchises consistently made good decisions, which repeatedly missed, and what trends define each front office’s drafting philosophy. Here are all the picks that the New York Giants made in the first round since 2020: Of the eight first-round picks that the Giants selected since 2020, Renner had four in the top third and four in the bottom third. Renner had this to say about the Giants’ assessment: There’s been no in-between for the Giants this decade. They’ve either nabbed franchise cornerstones or had complete whiffs. Now they just need those cornerstones to stay healthy. Jaxson Dart, Andrew Thomas and Malik Nabers have had their careers marred by injuries to date. If all are healthy this season, the Giants should finally make the leap to playoff contention. It’s difficult to disagree with the assessment. The four top-third selections came in Renner’s top 51 first-round picks of this exercise, with Jaxson Dart (pick 25) being the only one selected at a value (outside the top six). Carter, Dart, Thomas, and Nabers are all cornerstone players for the Giants. Three of the four players in the top third of Renner’s list for the Giants were selected by Joe Schoen, albeit the only players that weren’t were Andrew Thomas and Kadarius Toney. Both of Schoen’s first three picks in the first-round feel into the bottom third category. Thibodeaux is ranked 131st out of 191, but it’s not necessarily because he’s a bust. Although Kayvon Thibodeaux has earned 151 pressures across four NFL seasons, injuries have limited his availability and prevented him from fully living up to the expectations that come with being a top-five draft pick. He’s developed into a solid and productive edge rusher, but the 25-year-old must stay healthy to live up to his pedigree. Kadarius Toney was an insanely bad bust, and I’m surprised he’s only at 155, but the Giants — at least — traded back when they selected Toney. The Giants traded up for Banks, though, and he’s been a bust to date, although training camp reports are suggesting that he’s finding a groove with new defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson. Toney was ranked at 155, while Banks was at 161, but the latter can still return value on the pick. Evan Neal, somehow, can also return some value, although it’s unlikely. Neal was re-signed by the new regime but is no lock to make the roster. He is rightfully ranked at 185 out of 191 with former Giant Isaiah Simmons, tackle Isaiah Wilson, CB Jeff Okudah, and quarterbacks Anthony Richardson, Zach Wilson, and Trey Lance rounding out the poor end of Renner’s list. The top of the list Three players in the NFC East cracked the top ten of Renner’s list. Jayden Daniels ranked at number seven for the Commanders, with Micah Parsons, who is now a Green Bay Packer, coming in at eight. CeeDee Lamb was ranked tenth by Renner, as an excellent value in the middle of the first round ( 17th pick in 2020 ). Joe Burrow was the number one-ranked player, as the first-overall pick in the 2020 draft, with Drake Maye as the number two ( third selection in 2024 ). Justin Jefferson was the first non-quarterback at No. 3; he was selected at pick 22 by the Minnesota Vikings, with Jaxson Smith-Njigba at No. 4, as the 20th pick in the 2023 NFL Draft. Jordan Love rounded out the top five, as the 26th pick in 2020; finding a starting quarterback in the twenties was of high importance to this list, for obvious reasons. Abdul Carter is the first Giant on the list ( 38th ), with just one year under his belt. Wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan and center Tyler Linderbaum are ranked just ahead of Carter, with offensive tackle Charles Cross splitting Carter and Dart. Wide receiver DeVonta Smith was ranked at 41, just behind Dart, and Andrew Thomas was ranked 42nd. Final thoughts Renner is right. The Giants have either hit or busted on their first-round picks since 2020, with Kayvon Thibodeaux as an exception. Thibodeaux is not a bust, but he has yet to live up to the fifth-overall pick, despite solid play throughout his career. A year of health on his fifth-year option could dispel the bust narrative. His high draft capital more than likely pushed him to Renner’s ranking at 131 in the bottom third; he’s the third name in the bottom third, just behind offensive tackle Mekhi Becton and wide receiver Quentin Johnston, both of whom were selected outside the top ten. Still, the young edge defender must stay healthy The exercise was a fun thought experiment that analyzes the first round in a specific manner. Joe Schoen has done a better job finding quality contributors in the first round as the years have progressed, although the team’s struggles have led to multiple top-ten picks. Five of the eight selections were in the top ten. Schoen received two top-ten picks again, and both appear to be on the right track earning a spot outside of the bottom third. Both linebacker Arvell Reese and guard Francis Mauigoa must still prove their worth on the field — hopefully, for Schoen and all of our’s sake, they find themselves in the top-third next go around.

full_text: Dalen Cambre catching a pass during minicamp. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS W.Va. — Dalen Cambre caught 10 passes in a five-year career covering 63 games at Louisiana in the Sun Belt Conference. That is hard to believe when you watch the second-year wide receiver/special teams ace make catch after catch after catch, many of them spectacular, during New York Giants training camp in West Virginia. New head coach John Harbaugh has certainly noticed the 6-foot, 192-pound Cambre, who played seven games for the Giants last season after initially making the practice squad as an undrafted free agent. “I see him make a circus catch every single day,” Harbaugh said. “And not just that, he’s doing all the other things. He’s doing special teams. He knows what he’s doing. He’s running great routes. I think he’s making a move. I think he’s done a great job and he’s got our attention.” Cambre, a first-team All-American in 2024 as a special teamer, knew he would have to prove his mettle not only on special teams but as a receiver when he was signed by the Giants a season ago. “Coming in, I was told you have to be able to do everything,” Cambre said. “You’re not just going to have one guy that’s strictly special teams. He’s going to have to know everything. If he’s a defensive guy, he’s going to have to know everything on defense. He’s going to have to know everything on offense. And if he is truly just a special teams guy, he’s going to either be that one person on the roster or he’s going to have to do everything on special teams. It’s pretty rare you have just a special teams guy.” Cambre played 89 special teams snaps last season. He played 16 offensive snaps without a reception or a target. The 25-year-old said that with a new coaching staff this season, he feels like this is his rookie year all over again. “You go in as a rookie, and you’re like, I have to show these coaches who I am because, honestly, they didn’t know anything about me,” Cambre said on Thursday. “So I had to show them what I could do, who I am. “And then I got a new coaching staff, so it basically just started over. I told my family back home, I said, it’s rookie year two for me because [of the] new coaching staff. I’ve got to show them who I am, what I can do, and what I’m made of.” Judging from Harbaugh’s comments, it is clear that Cambre has done that. Throughout the Giants’ stay in West Virginia, it seems like Cambre, Odell Beckham Jr., and Braxton Berrios have separated themselves in the competition for spots at the bottom of the wide receiver depth chart. “Honestly, this receiver room, we’re really, really close. We are all getting along really, really well. We all have each other’s backs,” Cambre said. “Honestly, we’re like a little family in there. It’s pretty phenomenal.” Except, of course, that most of them are competing for non-guaranteed roster spots. Cambre understands that despite having Harbaugh’s attention, he doesn’t yet have a spot on Harbaugh’s season-opening 53-man roster. “It means a lot, knowing that you have, like you said, I have their attention,” Cambre said. “But that’s not the end of the day. You have to keep putting days together, stacking them day after day after day. “Because if I were to stop now, I mean, who knows? I’ve got to keep going, keep going each and every day and keep showing them what I can do, whether it be on special teams or in the receiver role.” Cambre has had to make himself into a real receiver. “It’s just been a grind each and every day. You really can’t see yourself as anything else. You have to envision yourself making those plays whenever you’re not practicing,” Cambre said. “You have to think about it. I go crazy sitting on the couch, and I’m thinking about, man, what if I do this, what if I do this? And then whenever I go to a workout, whether it be the offseason or on my own or something or before practice, and you have that opportunity, you already thought about it. “So you’re going out there like, man, I already lived this in my mind. I can go do this in real life.” The circus or acrobatic catch is not really something that can be directly practiced. So, how does Cambre try to prepare for moments when that is required? “It’s training harder than what it actually is because I do a lot of catching drills with tennis balls, one eye closed or behind a bag where you focus with one hand,” Cambre said. “You just put yourself in strenuous positions to be able to make the practices and the games easy because whenever a ball’s coming from way down the field, I mean, you have tons of time to move your body in ways to get to a better position to catch the ball. “Whenever you’re practicing at a strenuous level, those catches may seem easy, but, I mean, you’ve done it. You’ve repped the hard thing, so it looks and feels easy whenever it comes to you.” Cambre’s best catch of camp came during Monday’s torrential downpour, a staggering catch of a deep 50-50 ball from Jameis Winston against cornerback Korie Black. It never looked like a completion. Until Cambre caught it. Cambre broke the play down for me: “Honestly, I had a double move and ran a terrible route. Got a lot of correction on the route I ran itself. But when I turned around and looked for the ball, the ball was in the air. “And I noticed it was a little bit short. And I was thinking, man, the number one rule of a receiver is if you can’t catch the ball, no one can. So I was honestly thinking, okay, I’m just going to bat the ball down, live to go to second down. “And, honestly, I went to bat his hands down, hit the ball somehow, hit his hands down, and the ball just popped up. And it almost floated, like, right in my eye level. And whenever I saw that, I was like, oh, grab it. So I just grabbed it and then landed on top of him. And that’s just how it went.” If Cambre keeps making plays like that, the Giants are going to have a difficult time keeping him off the roster. Honestly.

title: Former Giant DJ Davidson retires
summary: Former New York Giants defensive tackle DJ Davidson has retired from the NFL. The announcement, such as it is, came courtesy of the NFL’s transaction wire when the Washington Commanders placed Davidson on the reserve/retired list. The Giants originally drafted Davidson out of Arizona State in the fifth round (147th overall) of the 2022 NFL […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants defensive tackle DJ Davidson goes for the ball against the Philadelphia Eagles | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Former New York Giants defensive tackle DJ Davidson has retired from the NFL. The announcement, such as it is, came courtesy of the NFL’s transaction wire when the Washington Commanders placed Davidson on the reserve/retired list. The Giants originally drafted Davidson out of Arizona State in the fifth round (147th overall) of the 2022 NFL Draft. He only played five games for the Giants as a rookie, suffering a torn ACL in the Giants win over the Green Bay Packers that year. The 6-foot-5, 320 pound Davidson was primarily a rotational nose tackle and special teams player for the Giants, appearing in 47 games with 4 starts in his four years as a Giant. The highlight of his career came in the Giants’ game against the Seattle Seahawks in 2024, when he sacked Seahawks’ QB Geno Smith twice in the Giants’ 29-20 win. Davidson signed a 1-year, $1.32 million contract with the Commanders back on April 1st, though only $20,000 of which was guaranteed. He finishes his career with 46 total tackles, 4.0 for a loss, and 2.5 sacks.

title: Giants sign center Brenden Jaimes as injuries pile up
summary: The New York Giants have officially signed center Brenden Jaimes (pronounced “HIGH-miss”) Jaimes, 27, was originally drafted by the Los Angeles Chargers out of Nebraska in the fifth round of the 2021 NFL Draft. He spent the first four years of his career on the Chargers, notably spending 2024 under Jim Harbaugh and Giants senior […]
full_text: Los Angeles Chargers offensive lineman Brenden Jaimes | Getty Images The New York Giants have officially signed center Brenden Jaimes (pronounced “HIGH-miss”) Jaimes, 27, was originally drafted by the Los Angeles Chargers out of Nebraska in the fifth round of the 2021 NFL Draft. He spent the first four years of his career on the Chargers, notably spending 2024 under Jim Harbaugh and Giants senior offensive assistant Greg Roman. He signed with the Tennessee Titans in 2025, but was released in final cutdowns and spent the 2025 season on the New England Patriots’ practice squad. He has appeared in 50 games over the course of his career, primarily as a special teams player, but also providing depth at guard and center. The decision to sign Jaimes comes as starting center John Michael Schmitz suffered ahead injury in practice on Friday, with head coach John Harbaugh saying Schmitz had his “bell rung”. At the same time, reserve center Lucas Patrick is dealing with a knee injury. Jaimes’ experience with Roman on the Chargers’ roster and Brian Callahan in the Titans’ training camp means he is likely at least familiar with the Giants’ blocking schemes and offensive terminology. That should allow him to step in and keep practice moving while Schmitz and Patrick recover. The Giants waived cornerback Jarrick Bernard-Converse with an injury designation to make room on the roster for Jaimes.

title: New York Giants mailbag: West Virginia, Evan Neal, placekicking, more
summary: Ron Corcillo asks: I’m curious about a somewhat overlooked aspect of this year’s placekicking battle: kickoffs. In particular, it occurs to me that Zvada, as a rookie, might struggle to adjust to the NFL kickoff rules, which could be a big factor considering the kind of field position you give up if you don’t place […]
full_text: Ron Corcillo asks: I’m curious about a somewhat overlooked aspect of this year’s placekicking battle: kickoffs. In particular, it occurs to me that Zvada, as a rookie, might struggle to adjust to the NFL kickoff rules, which could be a big factor considering the kind of field position you give up if you don’t place the ball in the landing zone. Have you seen any kickoff drills? Any intel on how the kickers are performing in that regard? Ed says: Ron, we really don’t see a whole lot of kickoff practice. When they do kickoff return/kickoff coverage they usually use the JUGS machine. I wouldn’t doubt that Dominic Zvada and Ben Sauls are practicing that skill during the early walk-through media does not see. Francis Castros asks: My number one concern on this team is the offensive line. I think there is depth but the two guys that concern me the most are JMS and Jon Runyan. Should I be concerned that the starting unit is Thomas, Runyan, JMS, Sisi and Eluemunor? Ed says: Francis, did you not notice that the offensive line, with four of those players you mentioned starting, played well last season? Runyan and John Michael Schmitz are not star players, but they are average NFL starters. Join the conversation! Sign up for a user account and get: Fewer ads Create community posts Comment on articles, community posts Rec comments, community posts New, improved notifications system! Brian Misdom asks: Hi Ed, as BBV and others have noted, the Giants have not allowed live updates during practice this training camp. How has this affected your approach to providing coverage compared to previous years where you could? Anything meaningfully different? If so, what are the pros and cons of the current set up? Ed says: Brian, the honest answer is that the policy is making my life easier. I’m not a young guy. I’m proficient with the technology, but not nearly as quick and capable as many of my younger cohorts. I have never liked tweeting during practice, though I understand the benefit for fans and the need to pass along injury information quickly. Why does the policy make it easier? Because my phone stays in my pocket. I don’t worry about firing off a tweet about the play I just saw, or something that comes to mind. When you are tweeting, your focus is not on the action taking place, and you miss things. Without having to tweet, I focus solely on what is happening on the field. It improves the quality of my notes, and, hopefully, the completeness of my practice reports and my understanding of what is going on. Bob Donnelly asks: Now that the trip to White Sulphur Springs is concluded I’d love to hear your thoughts on the overall experience. From the sports journalist perspective, other than being away from home for an extended period of time, was there any difference from the camps you covered at Quest Diagnostics Center? Did you get any sense of what the veteran players thought about camp being held at such a remote location? Ed says: Bob, this is a beautiful place. It is a different pace of life than what we are used to in the Northeast, but I can’t say it bothers me. It just takes getting used to. As for camp, players have enjoyed it. I know some of them wish there was more to do when they have time off. The flip side of that is it’s pretty hard to get into trouble. There will be an ‘Ed’s excellent West Virginia adventure’ post coming. So, look for that. Mike Winterode asks: Glad you are enjoying the beauty of West Virginia, it gets a bad rap that it doesn’t deserve. Question about Kayvon Thibodeaux. If he can stay healthy and has a good year, any chance the Giants re-sign him? He is a solid pass rusher and our best run defender on the edge. He was also on his way to having his best all around season last year before getting hurt, which to me, is the biggest knock against him. What do you think? Ed says: Mike, never say never. If Thibodeaux has a good year, he is going to get PAID by someone. The question is whether or not the Giants will be willing to get into an expensive bidding war. They are paying Brian Burns big money. They are going to have to do the same with Abdul Carter. How much money is too much at one position? It also won’t be long before they will be trying to get Jaxson Dart and Malik Nabers signed to long-term extensions. Lawrence Kenney asks: Very disappointed in this wasted, so far, Evan Neal draft pick. I was surprised they brought him back, but my question is if he’s playing on the third team and not spending time on the first team how will the Giants know if he’s worth keeping around. Unless he sees action against our best how can you determine his capabilities? Ed says: Lawrence, the coaching staff has watched Neal — and the other players — at every practice since early spring. They have evaluated the tape after each workout. If they felt Neal was deserving of more than third-team reps based on what they are seeing, he would be getting them. It is clear that the Giants are settled on their starting guards — Sisi Mauigoa and Jon Runyan. They have been with the first team since the spring. Reps as a unit are critical for an offensive line. We have seen, with disastrous consequences, what happens when an offensive line is unsettled and does not get to work together enough. The Giants do mix and match on occasion, with the first team working against the second or third team. So, backups do get occasional reps vs. starters. On padded practice days, there are also 1-on-1 blocking/pass rushing drills for players to try and impress coaches. Casey Sybrandy asks: How has Bobby Jamison-Travis looked in camp? Considering he may be the backup NT behind DJ Reader, I’d love to know if he’s flashed at all. Ed says: Casey, it has been a quiet camp for Jamison-Travis. That said, he is playing nose tackle and it is hard to focus on him from our vantage point during an 11-on-11 melee. We don’t have the luxury of being able to watch practice film, and it is impossible to focus on everything. Murray Krugman asks: Do you share my worry that Dart’s tone deaf foray into politics and sought-after pre-results celebrity as well as Skattaboo’s post-op WWE and not quite backflip suggest a possibly non teachable immaturity? Ed says: Murray, I do not. First, we were all young once. We all did dumb stuff. We all thought we already knew everything, until the world actually taught us that we didn’t. John Harbaugh has been around this block a few times. We already heard Cam Skattebo say he knows he has done dumb things at times, and that there won’t be any more back flips until he scores a touchdown in a game that counts. Dart works hard at his craft, and wants to win. That’s what matters. Do I wish he would tone it down sometimes? Sure. But, for better or worse the world has changed. He’s young. He has money. He has opportunities. He is living his best life. As for the political stuff, he is entitled to his views. I will be surprised, though, if we see that front and center again. Joe Gesell asks: After reading all the positive things about Greenbrier the last couple of weeks, I was wondering if there’s been any talk from the organization about returning there for future training camps? It sounds like it’s been a big hit with everyone from the coaches to the players. Of course that means you’d be forced to go too, you know, to cover camp & all. Ed says: Joe, I would not anticipate that. Renovations at the Giants’ facility will be continuing, so perhaps it is possible. The Giants, though, have everything they need at their own facility. If they can stay home, they will. Submit a question Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

title: Frank Reich thinks Geno Smith is in his prime
summary: Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich had big things to say about quarterback Geno Smith after a recent practice. “I don’t know how old he is. Isn’t he past 35?,” the offensive coordinator asked Friday before being told Smith is actually 35. “It feels like he’s 28. I’m telling you, it feels like physically, I see […]
full_text: FLORHAM PARK, NEW JERSEY - JULY 29: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets throws during training camp at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center on July 29, 2026 in Florham Park, New Jersey. (Photo by Adam Hunger/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich had big things to say about quarterback Geno Smith after a recent practice. “I don’t know how old he is. Isn’t he past 35?,” the offensive coordinator asked Friday before being told Smith is actually 35. “It feels like he’s 28. I’m telling you, it feels like physically, I see no … like, he is in his prime, physically.” “Like his arm, the way he moves, his feet in the pocket, he’s physically in his prime,” said Reich, in his first season running the Jets’ offense. “So he takes great care of himself and that’s going to help this team.” “Geno’s the leader,” Reich said. “He’s the leader of the offense, make no mistake about it, in every way, shape and form. And to me, what has become crystal clear in this early time in training camp, the attribute that sticks out to me is his laser focus. This man is laser focused like people don’t understand. Like, he comes to work and he is locked in. One thing that has been clear throughout the offseason is that the people running the Jets really believe Geno Smith has good football in front of him. While the cost to reacquire Smith was minimal, the team aggressively targeted him at the opening of the offseason, suggesting that he was their top choice rather than a fallback option. It probably goes without saying, but the accuracy of their assessment will go a long way in deciding whether this is a successful Jets season.

title: Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: A ton of observations from the longest practice of the summer
summary: Today marked the eighth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES UP NEXT: The Eagles have a rest day on Sunday before returning to practice on Monday morning at 10:00 AM Eastern.
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Saquon Barkley #26 of the Philadelphia Eagles smiles during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today marked the eighth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES The Eagles held a scrimmage today in what was their longest practice of camp. ‘Twas a grueling session in the hot summer heat. EAGLES INJURY REPORT: DID NOT PARTICIPATE: WR DeVonta Smith (hamstring) WR Makai Lemon (hamstring) WR Britain Covey (hamstring) S Cole Wisniewski (hamstring) EDGE Keyshawn James-Newby (ankle) LIMITED PARTICIPATION: LB Chance Campbell (groin) NOT ON THE TEAM-ISSUED INJURY REPORT BUT DIDN’T TAKE 100% OF THE REPS: OT Lane Johnson and OG Landon Dickerson were seemingly being load managed, which is sensible. Markel Bell rotated in at first-team right tackle and Drew Kendall rotated in at first-team left guard. Speaking of Lane, he revealed that 2026 is “probably” going to be his final NFL season . IN-PRACTICE INJURIES: C Cam Jurgens wasn’t listed on the injury report despite leaving Friday’s practice early. That was good to see. But Jurgens left practice early again for the second day in a row, albeit late in the session. Something to continue to monitor. Kendall took first-team center reps after Jurgens left. Depth running backs Elijah Mitchell and Dameon Pierce left practice early and did not return. JALEN HURTS UPDATE: Another practice from Hurts that left me more encouraged about his outlook than not. Stock up! THE GOOD: Hurts connected with a crossing Hollywood Brown on the right side of the field. If I’m nitpicking, the ball was slightly behind his target, but still entirely catchable. Hurts hit Brown again on a crosser, this time on the left side of the field in the red zone, for a catch-and-run touchdown with Saquon Barkley preventing Zack Baun from stopping the receiver short of the goal line. Hurts made a nice pre-snap read to recognize Wicks was going to be open between the hashes and the numbers. Hurts quickly put a ball on his target for a good gain. Hurts hit Wicks over the middle in stride for first down yardage. It’s clear that Hurts and Wicks have chemistry. And that’s crucial since Hurts has a tendency to especially lean into the targets he trusts … and avoid the ones he doesn’t. Hurts got the defensive line to bite on a pump fake that freed up a short dump off to Johnny Mundt. Hurts took a quarterback draw to the end zone. He’s looked pretty spry as a runner. Hurts completed a pass to Moore over the middle with timing. Hurts may have been “sacked” on this play … but he floated a ball to Goedert in the front right corner of the end zone that allowed the veteran tight end to make a jump ball grab at the catch point to beat Jihaad Campbell for a touchdown. Nice touch throw. Hurts found a crossing Moore in the end zone for a successful two-point conversion. THE BAD: Hurts threw the ball out of bounds on a rep where Wicks was open along the right sideline. Not sure if he sailed it or if it was a throwaway. Either way, it looked like there was a completion to be made and it wasn’t. Hurts was fortunate not to get picked off on a throw intended for Moore. The ball was floated short of his target and it looked like a diving Zack Baun was going to get the interception … but Moore ripped it out of the linebacker’s control at the last moment to bail out his quarterback. Really good catch. Baun did later intercept a Hurts pass. I can live with that mistake because it was an on-script throw and Hurts taking risks over the middle has been much more fruitful than not this summer. If this type of occasional turnover is the price to pay for an offense that’s more aggressive than it was last year, I think that’s a net positive. Saquon Barkley had some good runs today with the offensive line opening up holes for him. One such instance came when the Eagles’ offense was backed up against their own end zone and Barkley got freed up for a long touchdown run. Barkley found the end zone on a short run to cap off a successful drive by the offense. After scoring, Barkley went up to Cooper DeJean and got in his face to rub it in. Barkley then got into a shoving match with Quinyon Mitchell … but it looked more playful than truly heated. Fun to see some competitive intensity. Jordan Mailata was not flagged for what looked like a hold on a Barkley run to the left side but he probably should’ve been. Jalen Carter notched multiple “sacks” today, which is no surprise since he’s lived in the backfield all training camp long. The more I see from him, the more I believe he’s going to have a monster season. He looks ready to dominate. Jordan Davis also continues to look really good as both a run defender and a pass rusher. Jalyx Hunt flushed Hurts from the pocket by getting pressure from the right side of the offensive line. Jihaad Campbell had some really good run fits in this practice. That was good to see. I’m going to have to put myself in the “Losers” section of my next W-L-IDKs for not seeing offensive line versus defensive line 1-on-1s today. Not sure how I managed to get distracted and miss them. Bad job by me. Outsourcing: Just wrote out each of the OL/DL one-on-ones. Here are the key ones: – Jalyx Hunt nice inside move to beat Lane Johnson first rep – Tyler Steen great anchor vs Jalen Carter bullrush – Moro Ojomo beats Landon Dickerson with bend around the corner x2 – Markel Bell anchors well… — EJ Smith (@EJSmith94) August 8, 2026 Ty Robinson shows up today. He wins two one-on-ones vs. Drew Kendall. — Cayden Steele (@cayden_steele19) August 8, 2026 The highlight of OL vs. DL 1-on-1s was Willie Lampkin. He got three reps and shut down Gabe Hall twice at guard and then Zion Wilson from the center position. Lampkin plays with incredible (natural) leverage. Really fun to watch. — Dave Zangaro (@DZangaroNBCS) August 8, 2026 Willie Lampkin just had two really good reps vs. Gabe Hall in one on ones and is coming on in camp. Other highlights: Tyler Steen and Jalen Carter ruled a stalemate on their two reps; Markel Bell and Jalyx Hunt draw; Lane Johnson over Jalyx Hunt; Micah Morris over Uar Bernard. — Jeff Neiburg (@Jeff_Neiburg) August 8, 2026 Lampkin notably took reps at second-team right guard in addition to third-team center. The Eagles seem to be taking a long look at him, as they should be. I think Lampkin is going to crush the preseason and win a roster spot, small stature be damned. Every day after practice, the Eagles show "good effort" clips in a team meeting. Willie Lampkin is on those clips "all the time," Cole Payton said. "He's playing his ass off, and I'm super happy for him." — Brooks Kubena (@BKubena) August 8, 2026 Accounting for the above, Ty Robinson had his best practice as an Eagle. In addition to his success in 1-on-1s, he drew a false start penalty on John Ojukwu in team drills. He still has a lot of ground to make up but this was a positive step for the second-year defensive tackle. Michael Carter II knocked the ball out of E.J. Jenkins’ hands to force an incompletion. Relative to expectation, the Eagles’ top three safeties are looking good in camp. There’s always room to upgrade but I don’t think that position is in dire shape, which more than a minority have thought to be the case. Nolan Smith had good edge contain on a play where Hurts sprinted left looking for an easy completion … but instead was forced to throw the ball away. BACKUP QUARTERBACK BATTLE UPDATE: Continuing with the regular rotation, Andy Dalton was first up at quarterback with the second-team offense. Dalton should’ve had a good completion over the middle to an open Eli Stowers … but the rookie tight end coughed up the ball. Really bad drop. Dalton had a pass to Samari Toure knocked down by Tariq Castro-Fields … just not…

full_text: LANDOVER, MD - SEPTEMBER 21: Laremy Tunsil #78 of the Washington Commanders walks off of the field after an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Northwest Stadium on September 21, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Philadelphia Eagles host the Washington Commanders in Week 1, the Birds’ NFC East rival will be missing starting left tackle Laremy Tunsil. Tunsil suffered a torn triceps injury on Saturday morning that will reportedly cause the 32-year-old blocker to miss “ at least a significant portion of the regular season .” With the Eagles also set to play the Commanders in Week 8, it seems like Tunsil will miss both of Washington’s games against Philly this season. Tunsil is obviously one of the best players on the Commanders’ roster; he signed a contract extension that made him the NFL’s highest-paid offensive lineman on an annual basis earlier this year. Here’s how our frenemies over at Hogs Haven are reacting to this news: Reserve offensive lineman Andrew Wylie filled in at left tackle after Tunsil left practice, but he’s not the answer at left tackle. Brandon Coleman was in a position battle with Chris Paul to be the starting left guard, but Coleman’s likely the best option on the roster to move to left tackle. He made 12 starts at left tackle in 2024, before the Commanders traded for Tunsil in the 2025 offseason, and 15 over the last two years. Coleman will surely fill in there in the short term. The Commanders will monitor that performance closely before looking outside the organization for help. They also made mention of 2025 first-round pick Josh Conerly potentially switching from right tackle to the left side, where he played at Oregon. Regardless of how their replacement plan shakes out, this is a really big loss for the Commanders. The Eagles’ defensive line, which has looked really good in training camp, needs to take advantage of his absence.

title: Lane Johnson says the Eagles’ 2026 season will “probably” be his last year in the NFL
summary: Lane Johnson is “probably” going to retire after the 2026 NFL season. The Philadelphia Eagles’ two-time Super Bowl-winning right tackle unexpectedly revealed as much in his press conference following Saturday’s steamy training camp practice. Johnson, who previously met with the media early in camp, spoke to reporters for the first time after being excused for […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JUNE 9: Lane Johnson #65 of the Philadelphia Eagles talks to the media during mandatory minicamp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on June 9, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Lane Johnson is “probably” going to retire after the 2026 NFL season. The Philadelphia Eagles’ two-time Super Bowl-winning right tackle unexpectedly revealed as much in his press conference following Saturday’s steamy training camp practice. Johnson, who previously met with the media early in camp, spoke to reporters for the first time after being excused for four practices due to personal reasons. He touched on his reasoning for likely departing after this upcoming campaign: “As you get older, things change in your life. Priorities … your children get older, your parents get older. And, so, it puts things into perspective. So, [it’s] looking like this is probably potentially going to be probably my last year. Just ‘cause I am getting to that point of those priorities away from football are starting to merge. Not that I don’t enjoy— I love everything about this game and preparing for it. But that’s kind of where I’m at in my career. Yeah, man, just looking forward to this year, playing the best I can, and stay healthy. And that’s about it.” Johnson said he wanted to be “transparent” about his impending exit because it “allows [him] to kind of be at ease.” It’s impossible to say Johnson’s plan to walk away is a complete surprise. The 36-year-old is entering his 14th NFL season and there have been rumors about his potential retirement for multiple offseasons now. But it’s obviously notable for him to be so explicit about his intentions. Johnson was asked when he came to this decision: “I thought about it last year, really. Lots of conversations with my family, my kids. My oldest is turning 13 here in a few days. It’s hard to get time back. Especially, those years, are very pivotal. I think it’ll be a fun transition. But as far as my focus here, it’s with the Eagles, it’s playing. I still feel I can be a premier tackle in this league. My movement and everything, feels good. I just need to stay healthy and stacking days.” Johnson said the plan was always for him to return to the Eagles after his recent absence. He also mentioned his mom is “struggling with some health stuff.” Lane Johnson spoke about how he’s helping tend to health issues of mother, Ray Ann, and father, David. Ray Ann has been battling Hodgkin’s lymphoma. In 2023, I wrote about Lane’s strength in light of mental/physical strife. He gets it from his parents: https://t.co/MErWkDR3OV — Jeff McLane (@Jeff_McLane) August 8, 2026 In some ways, it’s hard to imagine the Eagles without Johnson being part of the team. He’s been a fixture of an historically successful era. He was the best blocker on two championship teams where the Eagles’ offensive line was a driving factor why the franchise lifted the Vince Lombardi Trophy twice. Johnson spoke on his legacy and how he wants to be remembered: “I just want to be known as, obviously, a great player but somebody that was always nice to kids, always nice to people in the [Eagles’] building. Hopefully somebody that elevated guys and was just a good teammate, fun to be around. Hopefully pick up guys when they’re not their best selves mentally. Give them some stories about some stuff I’ve overcome and handled. I want to be seen as a guy continually got better as he aged. Where some guys, once they hit 30, they kind of nose dive. Kind of the opposite of me. But, it’s lucky, man. Not everybody lands at a good organization where you have success and you have the ability to stack year upon year. So, I’m really fortunate, and I’m trying to soak in these last six months, seven months. For 2026, the Eagles can once again feel good about Johnson’s contributions as one of the very best offensive tackles in the league. Maybe they’ll even cap off his career with a third Super Bowl win. For 2027 and beyond, it remains to be seen how the Eagles will replace Johnson. His successor will likely be a downgrade, which isn’t even an indictment of them as much as it is a testament to how Johnson set the bar to an unreachable height. One potential option to become the Eagles’ next starting right tackle is Markel Bell. The 2026 third-round pick is massive and he’s been taking a lot of first-team reps. It’s possible that Bell could be the Eagles’ swing tackle this season before stepping up into a larger role as soon as next year. Johnson had some encouraging things to say about Bell’s outlook: “He’s been one of the best rookies I’ve been around, as far as being in the playbook, no complaining, haven’t heard him complain one time. He’s always asking questions. Just a really mature young man. Handles stuff off the field well. He’s just always asking questions. You can tell he was coached up well at Miami. I see a guy with that size and that ability and that wingspan and that movement, he can a lot of success in this business.” Whether it’s Bell or someone else, Johnson will leave massive shoes to fill assuming 2026 is truly the final season in his Hall of Fame caliber career.

summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles roster 2026: Updated locks, not-quite-locks, bubble players, and long shots – PhillyVoiceWR Darius Cooper ⬆️: Cooper has been the third-best receiver on the team throughout camp, and there’s a sizeable gap between him and whoever is fourth. full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 04: Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver Darius Cooper #80 runs a drill during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on August 4th, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Center in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles roster 2026: Updated locks, not-quite-locks, bubble players, and long shots – PhillyVoice WR Darius Cooper ⬆️: Cooper has been the third-best receiver on the team throughout camp, and there’s a sizeable gap between him and whoever is fourth. He is going to make the team. We’re bumping him all the way up from the bubble to lock status. He jumped two categories. […] WR Marquise Brown ⬇️: Brown got $5 million guaranteed from the Eagles, and he canceled out a comp pick. Also, he’s a legitimate, professional receiver with a track record of decent production. My opinion remains (mostly) unchanged that he’ll be on the team. However, I would have at least four receivers ahead of him on camp performance so far — DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Darius Cooper, and Elijah Moore. I might also add Johnny Wilson, and although Makai Lemon hasn’t done much he will obviously be on the roster. How many receivers can they keep? There should probably be some pressure for Brown to pick up his game. Eagles training camp: Lane Johnson returns, Jalen Hurts efficient on 28th birthday – The Athletic This was another strong practice from Darius Cooper, who is putting together a standout training camp (again). He’s not only positioning himself for a spot on the 53-man roster for the second consecutive year; he’s pushing his way into potential playing time at wide receiver. Hurts name-checked him without prompting during an NFL Network interview this week, and that should not be dismissed. Hurts is often intentional with what and who he discusses. Cooper had a strong rep against Quinyon Mitchell, an All-Pro cornerback. He makes contested catches, and he adjusts to the ball. It’s important not to overreact in either direction to a single practice, but when it happens over a series of practices, it’s hard to ignore. If I were making a 53-man roster today, I’d put Cooper over Johnny Wilson as the “dirty work” receiver. Perhaps there’s room for both. Even more, the idea of Cooper filling that role might need to shift if he keeps playing. He’s graduating from the plucky, small-school, undrafted-rookie storyline and is now in the conversation about how he can help the team. I remember when I covered the New York Giants in 2010 and 2011, Victor Cruz started to reconfigure the way he was viewed in Year 2 from that longshot who worked his way up the depth chart to a piece on offense. It might still be premature with Cooper, and Cruz is a lofty benchmark to hit, but you’re judged by the plays you make. Cooper keeps making plays. Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Backup quarterback battle heating up – BGN It was Tanner McKee’s turn to go up first with the second-team offense today. In terms of performance, McKee has been behind Andy Dalton thus far (though it’s been close) but today was the former’s best practice of the summer. Can Elijah Moore keep his career going with the Eagles? He’s trying to make the most of his extra reps. – Inquirer Asked Friday after the seventh practice of camp about his NFL journey, Moore was a little philosophical. “Life is not a linear path, I think, for any person,” Moore said. “There’s rarely — even some of the top players that get picked — that it goes exactly the way that they wanted. I think that’s there to teach you lessons. I’ve got kids. I got things I got to teach them outside of just having everything go my way. What example would I set if everything went my way? I wouldn’t have nothing to tell. I think it’s just brushing myself off, always having high hopes.” Right now, his hopes may be high for a reason. With DeVonta Smith and rookie Makai Lemon missing multiple practices with hamstring injuries, Moore has taken plenty of first-team reps and has flashed his abilities. It would be too strong to call him a camp standout, but his stock certainly is up from where it was before these seven camp practices. “I’m super critical of myself so I always think there is so much improvement that I could do with my alignment, my assignment, my execution,” said Moore, who has 209 catches, 2,274 yards, and nine touchdowns through five NFL seasons. “Am I making the most of my opportunities? Yeah. Is there still opportunities I’m leaving out there? Yeah. I always want to be perfect, as perfect as I can.” He may not be a starter, but Jeremiah Trotter sure looks like one – NBCSP The depth chart says he’s a backup. Practice reps say he’s a backup. Jeremiah Trotter sure isn’t playing like a backup. On an absolutely loaded defense, Trotter is enjoying a fantastic training camp as the top backup linebacker. In Year 3, Trott has a mastery of Vic Fangio’s scheme, and it’s showing up every day. He’s got these next-level football instincts that help him make up for late-round size and speed. He just always seems to know where the play is going both against the run and in coverage, and he’s never out of position. As good as he looked at training camp last summer, Trotter has taken a big leap this summer. “I think from last year, I definitely continue to improve myself physically,” he said after a recent practice. “I always try to make sure I’m in the best shape of my life because I want to make sure my teammates know that I’m grinding and working for them. Ranking 10 most interesting recent NFL contract extensions – ESPN 8) Jalen Carter, DT, Philadelphia Eagles. Here are players with the five most expensive contracts for a defensive tackle since 2015 in terms of APY adjusted for salary cap inflation: 1. Aaron Donald, 2022 ($45.8 million), 2. Ndamukong Suh, 2015 ($40.1 million), 3. Donald, 2018 ($38.2 million), 4. Carter, 2026 ($38 million), 5. Chris Jones, 2024 ($37.4 million). Are we sure Carter belongs on this list? On one hand, he has stretches where he takes over games and delivers impact plays. And he ranked third among defensive tackles in Fowler’s survey of coaches and executives. But Fowler also called him “one of the toughest evaluations among the top 10” and reiterated that with criticism from an NFL coordinator. The numbers don’t back Carter up as elite … yet. After registering a 90th percentile pass rush win rate along with six sacks as a rookie in 2023, his down-to-down metrics have fallen off. He dropped to the 52nd percentile (with 4.5 sacks) in 2024 and rebounded a bit to the 66th percentile (and three sacks) last season, though six pass breakups in each of those campaigns help his cause. Similarly, his run stop win rate was elite as a rookie and then just above average in each of the following two seasons. Carter has reached the Pro Bowl in each of the past two years and was a second-team All-Pro in 2024. He’s a very good player, especially if we’re looking forward (which we should be). But is he worthy of inclusion in the list above? It makes sense for the Eagles to want Carter on their roster for a long time. But the price feels steep. title: Asante Samuel Jr. is forcing himself into a major role with Steelers
summary: When the Pittsburgh Steelers took the practice field for the first time of training camp, they did so without Joey Porter Jr. and Jalen Ramsey. The two most vital pieces of the Steelers’ secondary were placed on the PUP list ahead of the team’s first practice – Ramsey dealing with a knee injury while Porter […]
full_text: May 28, 2026; Pittsburgh, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Asante Samuel Jr. (22) participates in OTA drills at the UPMC Rooney Sports Complex. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect When the Pittsburgh Steelers took the practice field for the first time of training camp, they did so without Joey Porter Jr. and Jalen Ramsey. The two most vital pieces of the Steelers’ secondary were placed on the PUP list ahead of the team’s first practice – Ramsey dealing with a knee injury while Porter was said to be nursing a bad back. As we head into Saturday’s night practice at Latrobe Memorial Stadium, neither Porter nor Ramsey have taken the field, leaving Pittsburgh in need of someone to step up. Asante Samuel Jr. has done just that. Through the first week and change of training camp practices, you could make a real and compelling argument that Samuel has been the best player on the field. He has consistently made terrific plays on the ball during team period, totaling several passes broken up at all levels, including a one-on-one ball while matched up with DK Metcalf on a deep pass from Aaron Rodgers. On Thursday, I asked head coach Mike McCarthy about Samuel and how impressed he’s been with him throughout this process. “[He’s made a] huge first impression with me,” McCarthy said. “Starting back in the spring… great energy all the way through the offseason program. I love his ball skills, his instincts, and his awareness. I think he’s had a great offseason [and] I think he’s having a better training camp.” With Ramsey not on the field, Pittsburgh has also had to toy with several defenders moving around in a version of their STAR role – one that Ramsey utilized in Los Angeles when he helped the Rams win Super Bowl LVI. During the offseason, defensive coordinator Patrick Graham said that Ramsey would play that STAR role in his defense. With the All-Pro cornerback off the field, that has allowed the Steelers to explore Samuel’s versatility. I asked McCarthy if he views Samuel as someone they can utilize both on the outside and at nickel, to which he answered with a resounding yes. “I think he’s definitely a position flexible player, clearly,” McCarthy said. The Steelers had Samuel fall into their laps as a free agent last season due to him undergoing spinal fusion surgery in April. The surgery was performed by David Okonkwo, who is the neurosurgeon for the Steelers. Once he was cleared in early November, the Steelers were quick to sign the former second-round pick who didn’t waste time showing that he was still a valuable asset. In Pittsburgh’s Week 15 contest against the Miami Dolphins, Samuel picked off Tua Tagovailoa to end Miami’s second drive, which kickstarted a Steelers’ rout of the Dolphins. While Miami scored late to make the final score more respectable, the Steelers held a 28-3 lead midway through the fourth quarter. They would go on to win 28-15. Now having a full offseason and new eyes on him, Samuel looks poised on building on a solid foundation that was laid in the final weeks of the 2025 season, but not just in a supporting role. No. 22 is single-handedly forcing himself into being a major player for Pittsburgh in 2026. Let us know what you think in the comments . Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more! full_text: DETROIT, MI - DECEMBER 04: Donovan Wilson #6 of the Dallas Cowboys defends in coverage during an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on December 4, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Steelers worked out six players over Thursday and Friday , PennLive’s Nick Farabaugh reported. Only one of those players, safety Israel Mukuamu , has been signed by the team so far. The other names to come to Pittsburgh were edges Xavier Thomas and Andre Carter II, safety Donovan Wilson, and wide receivers Cornell Powell and Isaiah Winstead. Thomas, Wilson and Powell are the most recognizable names. Thomas was a fifth-round pick in 2024 by the Arizona Cardinals out of Clemson. He scored a 6.79 RAS pre-draft as a sixth-year senior with 17.5 career college sacks, but never more than 3.5 in a season. He hasn’t recorded a tackle in an NFL regular season game since his 2.5-sack rookie campaign with Arizona. Wilson, like Mukuamu, is a former Cowboys safety, being drafted in the sixth round of 2019 by Dallas. He spent most of his NFL career being coached by Mike McCarthy. The 6’0, 204-pound defender is primarily a strong safety, with his best year coming in 2022: 101 tackles, five sacks, one interception and two passes defensed. The now-31-year-old started 15 games for the Cowboys in 2025. Powell is another Clemson product. He recorded 882 receiving yards and seven touchdowns in his final collegiate season before going in the fifth round of the 2021 NFL Draft to the Kansas City Chiefs. He scored a 7.59 RAS pre-draft, running a 4.53-second 40-yard dash. Powell has appeared in just three NFL games, mostly on special teams, with no career catches. He had a brief stint on the Steelers’ practice squad in 2025. The Steelers will finish Week 2 of training camp under the lights in an evening practice Aug. 8.

full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JULY 25: Jadarian Price #8 of the Seattle Seahawks reacts during practice at Virginia Mason Athletic Center on July 25, 2026 in Renton, Washington. Seattle has also dealt with the likes of high draft pick running backs Rashaad Penny and Kenneth Walker III missing parts of camp and/or preseason games due to injury as rookies. Head coach Mike Macdonald’s latest update on Price is still not that specific, but at least the timeline should calm any worried fans down. “We are going with a lower body soreness,” Macdonald said after Saturday’s Football Fest at Lumen Field. “Somewhere between the upper leg and lower body soreness. I’m not making light of it. It’s a minor issue right now. It’s a matter of days, so he will be back soon.” The Seahawks, meanwhile, signed running back Justin Jones presumably to just take some carries in upcoming practices while Price looks to return soon. The former Notre Dame back was on the sidelines at Football Fest after not being at Friday’s practice at all. With Price out, the bulk of the work at practice has gone to the trio of Emanuel Wilson, George Holani, and Velus Jones Jr. With Jacardia Wright also out injured, T.J. Harden has also taken some reps at the position. Seattle has an off-day on Monday before resuming practice on Tuesday for their preseason opener against the Dallas Cowboys.

full_text: We’ve reached the penultimate Seattle Seahawks public training camp practice, and it’s the big one at Lumen Field. Seahawks Football Fest has become a staple of August Seahawks football and serves as a prelude to the preseason. There will be a lot of family-friendly activities in and around the stadium, while something as close to simulating an actual game. As promised, the Seahawks Syndicate quartet of myself, Dan Viens, Bryce Coutts, and Brandon Cain (who’s will be LIVE from Fast Fashion Brewing in SoDo at 2:30 pm PT to preview the event, which is scheduled to start a little bit after 5 pm and end at around 7:30. It even still gives you time to watch the Mariners’ 50th anniversary special against the Tampa Bay Rays, although I imagine appetite is low right now. Field Gulls’ Josh Hite is also slated to come on as a guest analyst, so you get even more of a Field Gulls flavor! title: 10 things we learned from watching Day 12 of Seahawks training camp
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have been decidedly conservative with their training camp practices. Entering Saturday’s Lumen Field Football Fan Fest, the Super Bowl champs have held just three padded practices. We assume they’ll be in pads for Football Fest, but otherwise perhaps a combination of injuries and Mike Macdonald taking a different approach as reigning champions […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks have been decidedly conservative with their training camp practices. Entering Saturday’s Lumen Field Football Fan Fest, the Super Bowl champs have held just three padded practices. We assume they’ll be in pads for Football Fest, but otherwise perhaps a combination of injuries and Mike Macdonald taking a different approach as reigning champions has led to a change in how this year’s camp will look. Pads or no pads, there was still plenty to glean from Friday’s practice. Once again, I’m emptying the notebook with what I saw, with some extra eyes credited to Field Gulls’ Bryce Coutts and Seahawks Forever’s Dan Viens . Jadarian Price’s absence was Emanuel Wilson’s gain When the Seahawks signed Emanuel Wilson , it was just a “meh” for me, especially when Tyler Allgeier was on the free agent market. When he was with the Green Bay Packers, he looked like a solid backup with not much burst but a willingness to go north-south. Well, maybe that’s what John Schneider wanted. Wilson in run schemes where the goal is one cut and go north is a more than capable back. He’s shown good hands catching passes out in the flat, and I bet in padded practices he’d be pretty physical lowering his shoulder and plowing through defenders. Emanuel had a lot of first-team reps and looked good with his opportunities. Incidentally, the running game was better on Friday than Wednesday, and some of that might also have been going under center more as opposed to a lot of shotgun. Jadarian Price’s “lower body soreness” is not a major cause for concern yet and is worth monitoring, but I think Wilson was a Friday practice winner. Cooper Kupp is looking crisp When I was at camp last year, Cooper Kupp looked good and then wasn’t really that consistently good in the regular season. Come playoff time, Kupp looked close to his former Los Angeles Rams self. Perhaps time to heal from persistent injuries has given him a new lease on his football life, so to seapk. Kupp had a route-running clinic on Devon Witherspoon in one 1-on-1 rep and had a great catch against ‘Spoon in 11-on-11. Now, I don’t want to extrapolate from those two plays too much, but Kupp has drawn rave reviews throughout training camp. He looks healthier, his route running has always been crisp, and the one thing he has that I think Tory Horton is still developing is playing through the catch point. Horton has had some plays where he’s had the ball jarred loose at the point of contact, whereas whatever football Kupp grabs is staying grabbed. I think having Kupp still have some juice in this offense is beneficial for Horton, who isn’t under as much pressure to be thought of as a possible WR2. At the moment, I see Kupp and Rashid Shaheed as 2a/2b and Horton as WR4, which is totally fine. Ricky White III and Montorie Foster have stood out among the “other” receivers I mentioned this on Wednesday, but the WR6 competition is going to be really tight. Cody White is the established veteran at this point, such that it’d be no surprise if he’s waived and then put back on the practice squad again, but Ricky White III has really made a leap in terms of his route-running and catching in the offense. Jake Bobo being out has likely resulted in more of Ricky running with the twos, although he still gets time with the threes. When the third-team offense faced the first-team defense, Jalen Milroe threw a nice pass to Ricky, who hauled it in with Nehemiah Pritchett in coverage. Ricky caught a great back-shoulder catch on the sideline earlier with Drew Lock as the QB. Montorie Foster has also justified Seattle keeping him on a futures contract after spending all of last year on the practice squad. He may have a harder road to the active roster but at the very least, he will likely be back on the practice squad again this season. I don’t think any of Emmanuel Henderson, Irv Charles, or Rashad Rochelle has much of a chance to make it as a receiver. There’s a clear competition brewing for backup tackle… …But it’s not for Josh Jones’ spot. There’s no need to fret about Jones’ status as the top swing tackle on the team. Bobby Hart, who filled in for Jones during minicamp, has been chilling with the third-team offense and there’s almost no chance he’s on this roster come September. The other backup tackle situation is less certain. Amari Kight fared well in limited playing time in the tail-end of last season, but Kansas’ Logan Brown has really made a push and has gotten second-team offense reps at left tackle. Frankly, he’s looked better than Kight in both practices outside of a couple of false starts. Look out for Logan Brown to stake his claim for a roster spot. Brian Fleury will be using the tight ends and running backs a lot Seattle’s new offensive coordinator should lean into Shanahan Offense principles more so than Klint Kubiak ever did. Field Gulls’ Bryce Coutts did a great job of explaining this in his latest article. I’m not saying the Seahawks are going to make AJ Barner into Brock Bowers, but we will be seeing Barner and Elijah Arroyo’s route tree expand. I’m talking about Barner running an over route, or Arroyo lining up out wide, or (in Arroyo’s case) catching a shovel pass after a fake handoff from Sam Darnold. The TEs are also motioning constantly. The Seahawks’ situational drills involved a lot of quick passing against heavy pressure, which meant Darnold looking for a running back as an outlet. Whether that’s Emanuel Wilson or George Holani or even Velus Jones Jr, this was something that was worked on quite a bit. One wrinkle I liked was having Jaxon Smith-Njigba in the backfield (nothing new) but lining up Holani in the slot. There was a 21 personal shotgun formation with running backs on either side of Darnold. This offense is going to have a lot of things that are identical to last year, but there will be several wrinkles that will distinguish Fleury’s offense from Kubiak’s. The Jared Ivey “big EDGE” experiment is probably over Coming in at about 275 pounds, Ivey is theoretically a bit undersized as an interior defensive lineman but larger than your average edge rusher. There was intrigue last year when he stayed on the active roster the entire season, and he figured to factor into the competition again. After missing some practices due to injury, Ivey was lined up exclusively on the interior (at least, all the reps I saw). I think the reason Ivey is kicking inside has less to do with him and more to do with Rylie Mills being versatile enough to line up in a two-point stance and be an even bigger EDGE than Ivey. This, admittedly, may only make it harder for Ivey to make the roster this go-round. Mike Macdonald is working on his blitz packages Since this was not a simulated game type of practice, I won’t glean any indications that Macdonald wants to/is going to blitz more. However, as part of the situational 11-on-11s, it looked like there was a big push (particularly with the 1s) to have the offense have answers for Macdonald’s blitzes. One win for the defense was Ernest Jones blitzing Sam Darnold, with DeMarcus Lawrence coming unblocked and forcing a hurried throw over the middle to A.J. Barner. Drake Thomas picked off the pass and housed it. Seattle didn’t have to blitz much last year because the front four performed demolition jobs on a weekly basis. Whether that holds up this year remains to be seen, but don’t be surprised if part of Macdonald’s goal is to really unleash his full defensive call sheet and dial up some extra pressure. Jalan Gaines continues to make plays In our Wednesday recap, we noted that the edge rushing depth failed to impress . If you remember Jalen Gaines from last year, he blocked the winning field goal that preserved a tied outcome with Pete Carroll’s Las Vegas Raiders in preseason. Gaines has shown some flashes of pass rush potential, including a would-be sack after once again not biting on a play-action fake, as well as just owning Bryce Cabeldue on another 11-on-11 rep. I’m…

title: August quotes and hope for more Seahawks offensive line growth
summary: There has been no shortage of ink spilled discussing how a full offseason of Rashid Shaheed could take the Seattle Seahawks offense to the next level. A healthy Tory Horton and a growing Jadarian Price are both exciting x-factors to consider. For all of the weapons that could get more and more lethal as they […]
full_text: There has been no shortage of ink spilled discussing how a full offseason of Rashid Shaheed could take the Seattle Seahawks offense to the next level. A healthy Tory Horton and a growing Jadarian Price are both exciting x-factors to consider. For all of the weapons that could get more and more lethal as they gel, the offensive line in Seattle could be entering a golden age. Mike Macdonald spoke at the NFL Combine about the impact of the previous rookie class (and Grey Zabel, in particular) in winning a title in 2025: “Look at the productivity we had of those top two guys, solidifying our offensive line with Grey. And really, the leadership position that he’s taken within our team was really integral to our success on offense.” Field Gulls’ own Alexandre Castro did a great breakdown of what makes Zabel special at left guard and how he can turn it up a notch. The Seahawks were top five in fewest sacks allowed on offense and saw the ground game spring to life later in the year. When asked about the offensive scheme continuity from year to year, Grey had this to say : “Quite a bit of carryover. I think it’s the similarity of last year that helps us play fast and understand the offense really well. But there’s a lot of new things, twists to the offense that allows us to gain a little bit more knowledge of the defense and what they’re doing and then be in the best play possible.” He’s CHASING EDGES, ladies and gentlemen!!! His fellow lineman agrees with him. Right tackle, Abraham Lucas on how the continuity on the offensive line and with the offensive system helps the O-linemen: “I think it’s pretty night and day from where we started out last year. Speaking for myself, it’s much, much more confident, in like the play calling and running the plays. Just because when we were starting up last year, you’re still kind of learning all the calls and the adjustments and then going out and executing all of them after a day of install. And now we’ve had basically a whole year of install.” Do we dare give ourselves hope, by considering what it would look like if this offensive line took another big step this season? View Link The national media has written Seattle off already, due to free agency and coaching hire losses. The Seahawks all seem to be pretty comfortable with the new OC to replace Klint Kubiak, however (as much as you can be before the bullets actually start flying). Aden Durde (defensive coordinator) was asked about the offense making some plays in training camp: “I think because there’s a lot of carryover.” He expounds on that thought from there, saying that “there’s an understanding of how the rules are-targeting… but they’re doing a great job. The detail’s there, and they’re creating explosives. They’re giving us problems at times. I thought today was a great practice.” Brian Fleury (the aforementioned new offensive coordinator on the offensive line continuity: “It’s an extremely rare situation to have all five starters returning, especially from a Super Bowl team. So, I’m walking into a really good situation. And then, I’ve worked with (offensive line coach) John Benton before. He does a phenomenal job of coaching that group, so the cohesion that they already have just makes it really, really easy to implement stuff. Then, when you do realize that an adjustment needs to be made, they’re just so used to working with each other and communicating that adjustments happen lightning fast. So that’s a nice advantage to that situation.” That’s definitely reassuring to hear. In a world where championship rosters often get pilfered. The line’s leader, left tackle Charles Cross , gave Benton some flowers, saying that “he’s a very detail-oriented guy. Gives us a lot of clarity. No gray area.” I can’t be sure, but I don’t think that pun was intended. What is obvious, however, is that improvement in the OL room is a group project, and all seem to have a shared vision for what they can do in 2026. Cross said that they are “continuing to build.” Right guard, Anthony Bradford , in a contract year, said in an interview with Corbin Smith that he is focused on “how can we stack what we did last year and make it even better?” These guys are all saying the right things. Including the guy with potentially the most on the line (pun intended). Fleury spoke to his feelings on the blitz pickup and blitz recognition against Mike Macdonald’s defense: “I think it was pretty good today.” He goes on to mention how “Sam, particularly, that’s a great job of recognizing those things and getting us into the best possible scenario.” That right there is an interesting thought to keep in play. Not just the hopeful improvement of an O-line that returns all of their starters… but the efficiency that could come from the signal caller having a stronger and deeper command of the whole operation. The oft alluded to “continuity” along the protecting wall we be even further tested soon. This might be a real-time case study in how much that actually helps a young group get better together. The heat of joint practice against the Tennessee Titans (at Vanderbilt) should provide a good litmus test before the campaign begins. Joint practice with the #seahawks coming up https://t.co/OIGi4z6Y1v — Curtis Allen (@curtis93969) August 4, 2026 Do I need to remind anyone what Jeffery Simmons did to Laken Tomlinson before Grey Zabel was a thing? That man is still holding it down in Tennessee, this time with Robert Saleh at his back. Jeffery Simmons tosses Laken Tomlinson out the club at #Titans / #Seahawks joint practice today (🎥: Dylan Bradley IG) pic.twitter.com/ryEnfdKdhA — Wes Wisley (@TitansStats) August 16, 2024 If the offense steps up to cover for any falloff from a historic defense, the development of the offensive line will most likely play a huge part. Let’s hope the line can hold up as a whole, and individually this year. If they can stay healthy, improve just a little bit, and keep Sam Darnold healthy and protected, this team can continue to be a contender. If they can improve a lot? Well, the sky would be the limit for Cross, Zabel, Jalen Sundell, Bradford and Lucas.

full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys. There are years, like 2010, when the Seattle Seahawks have thanked the football gods that they resided in the NFC West, however they’ve been few and far between recently. From the meteoric rise of the Los Angeles Rams to the revival of the San Francisco 49ers, this year’s NFC West is shaping up to be one of the most difficult divisions in football. Yet, Seahawks fans don’t seem too concerned with the offseason noise. In our weekly survey of the 12s, a majority predicted that the Seahawks will go 5-1 in the NFC West in 2026. Here are the results. Only 9% of fans expect perfection from the reigning Super Bowl Champions; most fans are not too far off. A 5-1 record in the division would improve on what the Seahawks did a year ago, when a 4-2 record and several heart attacks against the Rams were enough to clinch the division title. While I can’t confirm this, I have an inkling that most fans who voted for the 5-1 outcome did so because they have little faith in the 49ers, who are dealing with a gluttony of injuries and struggled mightily against Mike Macdonald-led defenses. Around 36% of fans appear to be realists and expect their performance from a year ago to carry over, likely dropping a game each to the 49ers and Rams. The Seahawks did land a tough draw playing the Rams two times in three weeks toward the end of the season, which does leave room for doubt, as it’s harder to predict what the Seahawks will look like in December What jumps out to me more than the records is the fact that 96% of Seahawks fans believe their team will have a positive record in the NFC West, a staggering vote of confidence in the team. Well, that’s for this week, but don’t let this discussion die here. How do you think the Seahawks will perform in the NFC West? Who might they drop games to? full_text: The Seattle Seahawks held their eighth public training camp practices early Friday morning, a special practice for season ticket holders and their guests. It was another warm day at team headquarters in Renton, albeit less smoky and hazy than earlier in the week. Much like Wednesday’s practice, the Seahawks were not in pads, and indeed they mixed things up with the 11 vs. 11 sessions. There was first-team offense vs. second-team defense, third-team offense vs. first-team defense, the usual 1s vs. 1s and 2s vs. 2s, plus a lot of situational football like red zone and 3rd-and-long work that often decides actual games. For the second time this week, Field Gulls was on-site at VMAC observing what was just about a three-hour long practice. Myself and fellow Field Gulls staff writer and host of The Hawks Eye podcast , Bryce Coutts, as well as Seahawks Forever podcast host , Dan Viens, filmed an instant reaction video after practice ended with our quick-fire takeaways. We discuss the absence of Jadarian Price ( which we now know is due to “lower body soreness” per Gregg Bell ), the impressive performances of Emanuel Wilson and Ricky White III, a name to watch at the edge, and a promised wrinkle in Brian Fleury’s offense that we saw heavily worked on in today’s practice. full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 08: (L-R) Larry Fitzgerald, Adam Vinatieri, Luke Kuechly, Roger Craig and Drew Brees pose for photos during the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Enshrinement Ceremony at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 08, 2026 in Canton, Ohio.
